Once the classifier has been rebalanced, however, final accuracy does not reveal whether further encoder adaptation remains worthwhile. Standard imbalance benchmarks obscure this question because they jointly vary the number of distinct examples available to rare classes and the frequency with which those examples shape the representation. We introduce a controlled evaluation framework that separates unique support from representation allocation and estimates the incremental value of encoder updates through matched classifier-only and full-network continuations from a common corrected model. The framework combines stage-specific controls, multiple representation and adaptation objectives, whole-distribution metrics, and hierarchical inference over class assignments, support reconstructions, and optimization runs. Across the controlled study, the same low-support regime moves from one in which classifier-only training is adequate to one in which encoder adaptation yields a practically meaningful benefit solely as representation allocation becomes more imbalanced. The transition persists across classifier corrections, representation objectives, normalization and augmentation controls, and ImageNet-scale evaluation, while preserving frequent-class accuracy. Under the prespecified one-percentage-point operating margin, the two regimes are separated by simultaneous confidence bounds. These results show that benchmark construction can alter a post-correction training decision and that support size alone does not characterize the remaining value of representation adaptation.

arXiv.title: Capability-Conditioned Graph Control Barrier Functions for Zero-Shot Safe Navigation of Heterogeneous Mobile Robot Teams
arXiv.abstract: Multi-robot systems are increasingly deployed as heterogeneous fleets with diverse kinematic and actuation capabilities. While graph control barrier function (GCBF) methods provide a scalable framework for decentralized safe control, existing approaches typically assume homogeneous robot dynamics. Methods that directly encode robot classes can distinguish known types, but do not represent state-dependent motion capabilities or naturally transfer to unseen robot models. To address this challenge, we propose the Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier Function (CC-HGCBF), defined in a shared second-order reference-point operational space. This formulation provides a common geometric representation of safety across heterogeneous robots while retaining their model-specific dynamics and admissible control constraints. To enable zero-shot transfer, we introduce the Radial Capability Field (RCF), a compact, fixed-dimensional representation of each robot's state-dependent finite-horizon reachable velocity set. Conditioning the shared graph barrier and decentralized policy on the RCF enables them to adapt to changes in robot state, kinematic constraints, and control limits without relying on predefined robot identities. We jointly train the barrier and policy using proactive safety labeling and neural CBF-QP supervision, and evaluate them on mixed teams containing both seen and unseen robot models. Experiments demonstrate scalable safe coordination and zero-shot transfer to robot models and capability variations withheld during training. Physical-robot experiments further demonstrate zero-shot deployment to unseen kinematic models without retraining.

arXiv.title: Beyond Response Scoring: An AI-aware Cognitive Supervision Framework for Automated Mathematical Short Answer Grading
arXiv.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.

arXiv.title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents
arXiv.abstract: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.

arXiv.title: A Positional Realizability Theory of Length Generalization in Single-Head Attention
arXiv.comments: 26 pages, 6 figures. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), October 2026. Code available at https://github.com/superajgklasjglaks/positional-realizability
arXiv.journal-ref: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), October 2026
arXiv.abstract: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $α_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(Φ, t_n)$ alone. Here $α_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $α_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $α_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.

arXiv.title: DistFlow and Its Conic Relaxation: Regularity, Monotonicity, and Hybrid Exactness via Graph Decomposition
arXiv.abstract: Classical exactness conditions for conic relaxations of the DistFlow model rely, among other assumptions, either on all nodal injections being adjustable or on a network-wide path condition. In practice, these conditions may not hold uniformly across a feeder: controllable distributed energy resources (DERs) sit at some buses and fixed loads at others, while reverse flows from DER-rich regions can violate the path condition. This paper certifies exactness region by region and composes the regional certificates, accounting for perturbations that propagate downstream through voltages. We first introduce a subtree voltage stability region, in which the network and all compatible subtrees remain regular. Within it, two endpoint sign conditions, one relaxing the nonnegative-flow assumption and one implied by the classical path condition, yield monotone responses of voltages, currents, and losses to root voltages. Using duality, the implicit function theorem, and sign properties of inverse sensitivity matrices, we recast both classical arguments as individual sign certificates on branch multipliers. This turns exactness into a branchwise property that can be certified region by region. A partition rule then splits the network into dispatchable and passive subtrees, and a hybrid certificate combines their local conditions into exactness of the full-network relaxation, under additional operating-limit and objective conditions. In particular, placing controllable DERs at both ends of a branch with large reverse flow exempts that branch from the passive sign conditions.

arXiv.title: Control-Layer Interpretation of Reactive Power Recovery Limits in EMT-RMS Model Benchmarking of Inverter-Based Resources
arXiv.comments: Accepted for presentation at IEEE PES Grid Edge Technologies 2027, April 19-22, 2027, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA.5 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
arXiv.abstract: EMT--RMS benchmarking is widely used to verify cross-platform consistency of inverter-based resource (IBR) dynamic models. This paper examines a 200 MW anonymized IBR represented in PSCAD and PSS/E. The EMT model separates inverter electrical capability from a plant-level power plant controller (PPC) recovery target, whereas the RMS model represents these functions through REECC and REPCA parameters. Directly assigning the PPC target of $\pm 0.2764$ pu to REPCA hard reactive limits is initialization-inconsistent at the original lagging operating point because the initial reactive command is 0.396273 pu. A second, near-unity-power-factor operating point initializes successfully with the same diagnostic limit, demonstrating that the conflict is operating-point dependent. Using the non-conflicting capability mapping removes the original hard-limit conflict, but the benchmark still shows 18.5--30.2 MVAr post-event POI reactive-power differences from PSCAD. A one-at-a-time REPCA $K_c$ sensitivity under matched benchmark initial conditions further shows that RMS recovery is parameter- and limit-dependent: at $K_c=0.05$ and 0.10 the aggregate machine reactive output reaches the configured capability bounds, while $K_c=0.15$ moves VDOWN, VUP, and HVRT off those bounds and changes their settled POI reactive power by 8.94, 18.00, and 3.17 MVAr, respectively. Machine-to-POI accounting further shows why machine-side saturation need not reproduce the POI-level PPC recovery magnitude. The results distinguish initialization feasibility from recovery equivalence and provide a control-layer diagnostic workflow beyond waveform comparison.

arXiv.title: Corroborative Learning: Mutual Enhancement through Task-Response Reconstruction
arXiv.abstract: In pattern analysis, models trained independently for the same task often develop complementary capabilities through differences in architecture, data, and optimization. Exploiting complementarity while retaining independent deployment is central to collaborative learning. Most methods establish transfer by reducing differences in predictions, relations, or representations between target and collaborator, although these differences also underlie complementarity. This creates a structural trade-off between reducing differences for knowledge exchange and preserving them for complementarity. We therefore propose Corroborative Learning (CL). Each model forms task-driven responses, with cross-group support from its collaborator. Source-excluded reconstruction of response increments from collaborator representations separates fitting and evaluation across disjoint groups and selectively constrains directions by cross-group reconstructability. The process requires no direct output or feature matching or additional inference dependency. Furthermore, with linear reconstruction and fixed collaborator representations, the loss equals a positive semidefinite directional regularizer, constraining less reconstructable directions more strongly. Signal and noise conditions characterize when directional shrinkage reduces response-estimation error. Across six language tasks, 24 models, and 36 pairs, CL improves over capacity-matched independent adaptation on every task, with positive gains across most directed model combinations. Pairwise comparisons show broad advantages over transfer and mutual-learning methods and different gains from complementarity across collaboration rules. Low-label language and vision results support cross-domain applicability. Task-relevant differences can support mutual enhancement without eliminating disagreement.

arXiv.title: RTL-Interact: Training EDA-Interactive Models for Multi-Task RTL Design
arXiv.abstract: Large language models offer a promising route to register-transfer-level (RTL) design, but reliable implementations require checking and revision based on electronic design automation (EDA) tools' feedback. Existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such EDA tools or rely on separate generation and repair components. We introduce RTL-Interact, a multi-task post-training framework that trains a single RTL-specialized model to generate RTL, construct task-appropriate EDA checks, and revise implementations using tool feedback. The framework combines automatically constructed multi-task demonstrations with staged supervision from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning. We further introduce Pattern-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) for multi-task reinforcement learning. PAPO augments Group Relative Policy Optimization with correctness-gated rewards that favor concise successful checking while rewarding effective revision, and uses task grouping to preserve coverage across objectives. On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B achieves 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5, surpassing its teacher model, DeepSeek-V3.2, while RTL-Interact-8B achieves 44.9% weighted Pass@1. Additionally, we show that PAPO can reduce average tool calls by 63.8% while improving Pass@1. Both models also outperform all RTL-specialized baselines on VerilogEval v2 and RTLLM v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method.

arXiv.title: Imputing Missing Data in Longitudinal Life-Logging Athlete Data
arXiv.abstract: Long-term, diverse personal informatics data enables athletes to understand and act on their health and performance goals, whether assessing readiness right now, tracking how soreness relates to training load over time, or predicting how sleep affects next-day performance. However, the inherent missingness in longitudinal data, if handled inappropriately, can bias these analyses. To our knowledge, no prior work has systematically benchmarked classical and deep learning imputation methods on long-term self-tracking data from athlete populations. We evaluate six imputation methods across four missingness mechanisms at missingness rates spanning 10-80%. Using seven diverse long-term self-tracking datasets from 231 individuals, we assess both point accuracy and the preservation of temporal and multivariate structure. Our results show that no single method dominates across all conditions and reveal a critical trade-off: while PAIN is superior on point-wise accuracy, deep learning methods (BRITS, GRU-D, and GRIN) are better at preserving multivariate and temporal structure, particularly under higher missingness. Our findings offer a practical, goal-conditioned framework that guides researchers in selecting imputation strategies aligned with both the underlying missingness mechanism and the specific analytical goal of long-term self-tracking studies.

arXiv.title: Delta-Seeker: Closed-Loop Generative Search for Novel Circuit Design Discovery
arXiv.abstract: Generative models are increasingly used for circuit synthesis and optimization by proposing topologies, sizing devices, and exploring large design spaces. We investigate whether they can instead support design discovery, where generated structures must depart from known designs while producing reproducible electrical behavior. We propose Delta-Seeker, a closed-loop circuit search framework that combines discrete diffusion for topology generation and mutation with structural checking, SPICE-in-the-loop sizing, Pareto selection, and feedback from prior search outcomes. The search controller uses progress and recurring structural failures to allocate evaluation effort and steer subsequent topology generation, while independent re-sizing and operating-corner analysis are performed only after search. In generator-only experiments, cross-generation feedback increases structurally valid children from 143 to 945 and reduces the faulty-candidate fraction from 0.925 to 0.761. In op-amp topology discovery at matched sizing cost, Delta-Seeker yields 54 designs that remain feasible in at least three of four independent re-sizings and 18 that additionally pass device-level checks and supply-temperature corner analysis, compared with 38 and 10 under fixed control. Removing cross-generation memory reduces independently robust discoveries from 54 to 43 and seven-corner robust discoveries from 40 to 27. In DC-DC converter search, nearest-parent analysis identifies a corpus-absent topology whose generated switching current path changes its nearest training-corpus parent from infeasible at all four operating corners to feasible at all four, while increasing median efficiency from 31.2% to 98.96%. These results show that closed-loop generative search can support circuit discovery beyond structural novelty by identifying new topologies with independently verified changes in circuit operation.

arXiv.title: Evolution of Financial AI: From Statistical Models to Agentic AI
arXiv.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in finance has evolved from statistical learning and machine learning for structured prediction, through deep learning and foundation models for representation learning, language understanding, and reasoning, to retrieval-augmented generation for knowledge-grounded reasoning and agentic AI for autonomous planning and execution. In this paper, we examine how researchers and practitioners can select and apply AI methods in finance. We first show that the major paradigms of financial AI address fundamentally different classes of problems, rather than forming a strict hierarchy of capability. We then review the current state of research on AI in finance and trace how these paradigms have reshaped financial data, financial tasks, decision support, and human-AI collaboration. Building on this, we propose practical guidelines for matching AI paradigms to task characteristics, and show that more advanced models, such as foundation models or autonomous agents, are not universally superior. We conclude by outlining open challenges for researchers and practitioners working toward reliable financial AI.

arXiv.title: Coarse3D: Controllable and Faithful Sparse Structure Generation for Image-to-3D
arXiv.abstract: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

arXiv.title: TRIDENT and SHAKTI: A Framework and Benchmark for Hindi AI-Text Detection
arXiv.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly multilingual, distinguishing human-written from AI-generated text is essential for maintaining information integrity. However, research remains English-centric, with limited benchmarks for low-resource languages such as Hindi. To address this gap, we introduce SHAKTI, a large-scale Hindi benchmark covering four genres, eight LLM families, multiple prompting strategies, and adversarial transformations. We evaluate its quality through human annotation and analyze linguistic, grammatical, and sentiment-based differences between human- and AI-generated texts. Building on these findings, we propose TRIDENT, a round-trip translation-based detection framework with three variants: TRIDENT-S (static threshold), TRIDENT-D (dynamic threshold), and TRIDENT-C (logistic regression using multi-distance RTT features). TRIDENT leverages semantic consistency between original and round-trip translated texts to identify AI-generated content. Extensive experiments show that TRIDENT outperforms conventional and supervised baselines, with TRIDENT-S achieving the best overall performance. Further evaluations across seven languages, adversarial settings, and unseen LLMs demonstrate its multilingual applicability and robustness, while highlighting sensitivity to the translation model.

arXiv.title: CONSORT: Uncertainty-Constrained Multi-Robot Planning for Cooperative Localization in GPS-Denied Environments
arXiv.abstract: Centralized multi-agent path planning with cooperative localization in GPS-denied environments is generally computationally intractable when formulated in full belief space due to tightly coupled uncertainty dynamics. Prior work typically approximates belief dynamics or restricts inter-agent coupling. This work examines a multi-agent planning problem in which a primary agent must reach a goal in minimum time subject to a chance-constrained collision-avoidance requirement and a terminal bound on localization uncertainty. We obtain a tractable surrogate of the underlying belief-space problem by optimizing over the mean-state trajectories of all agents and propagating covariance for terminal constraint evaluation only. We propose CONSORT (Cooperative Navigation with Support-Optimized Routing and Trajectories), a discrete-to-continuous pipeline combining hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based trajectory refinement. Across 50 randomized scenarios, the planners separate as the terminal uncertainty bound tightens, with CONSORT solving 80% of scenarios where the strongest baseline solves 54%, at comparable path length. In marine simulations, with the plans executed under feedback control on an independently developed factor-graph estimate, the trajectories remain collision-free and their terminal uncertainty falls within 6% of the planner's prediction.

arXiv.title: Experts Exhibit Structured Redundancy: Structure-Preserving Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
arXiv.abstract: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.

arXiv.title: Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning for BESS Dispatch Under Renewable Uncertainty
arXiv.abstract: Battery energy storage system (BESS) flexibility depends on state of charge and intertemporal operating constraints. Renewable forecast errors of similar magnitudes can lead to different BESS dispatch results. An error may alter early charging or discharging decisions and reduce the flexibility available for subsequent regulation, while another may have little effect on the resulting schedule. To account for these unequal consequences, this paper proposes Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning (FC-DFL), which trains renewable predictors using the realized operating costs of their induced BESS schedules. Gaussian smoothing and solver-based zeroth-order estimation provide training feedback without requiring differentiating through the non-differentiable mixed-integer BESS dispatch problem. The same decision feedback is further combined with prediction sensitivity to develop a decision-oriented XAI method that identifies the input features and forecast periods most consequential to BESS operation. Case studies using German wind and solar data show that FC-DFL reduces the integrated absolute frequency-deviation metric by 6.05% and decision regret by 23.92% relative to accuracy-based predict-then-optimize method. The XAI analysis further demonstrates that the identified high-impact forecast periods produce 2.84 times larger average absolute changes in realized operating cost than low-impact periods. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating downstream decision-making outcomes into renewable forecasting and demonstrate the value of FC-DFL in improving BESS regulation and providing operationally meaningful forecast explanations.

arXiv.title: Understanding LLM-Based Bargaining of Driving Agents in Mixed-Autonomy Traffic
arXiv.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a flexible computational approach for modeling social interactions among heterogeneous agents. This paper develops a novel framework towards characterizing and understanding LLM-based population-level bargaining of shared road space between autonomous vehicle (AV) and human-driven vehicle (HV) agents in mixed-autonomy traffic. Through controlled experiments varying traffic density, agent objectives, and traffic-domain knowledge, we first characterize bargaining outcomes and observe heterogeneous agreement rates across different experimental conditions. To understand how the bargaining process shapes the outcomes, we introduce a behavioral taxonomy that jointly characterizes numerical bidding actions and communicative attitudes. We examine two complementary aspects of social interaction: inter-agent bargaining dynamics and private-to-public behavioral transformation. Results reveal distinct interaction patterns associated with agreement and breakdown, including greater constructive reciprocity in agreement trials and more frequent conflict escalation in breakdown trials. Furthermore, private and public communicative attitudes often differ even when numerical bids remain unchanged. These findings illustrate how LLM-based bargaining simulations can support a structured analysis of social interaction behaviors in mixed-autonomy traffic.

arXiv.title: Generative SDEs with Trainable Diffusion and Density-Based Losses
arXiv.abstract: We develop a divergence-kernel method for jointly optimizing neural SDE drift and diffusion fields and the initial Gaussian distribution, using losses that depend directly on the terminal density. In two- and eight-dimensional Gaussian-mixture experiments, we learn time-independent fields and obtain far fewer off-mode samples than score-based generators with similar parameter counts. The drift attracts samples toward the modes, while the diffusion helps disperse excess probability between them.

arXiv.title: A Unified Framework for Probability Estimation of Data-Dependent Events
arXiv.abstract: We study the general problem of estimating $D(\dde(S))$, the probability that an unknown distribution $D$ assigns to an event determined by a sample $S$ of $n$ i.i.d.\ draws from $D$ through a known mapping $\dde$. The estimation algorithm knows $\dde$ and $S$ but does not have access to any additional samples from $D$. This formulation captures classical missing mass, the data-dependent targets of adaptive data analysis and post-selection inference, and the test error of a data-trained predictor, whose estimation was recently studied by \new{Gastpar et al.\ (2024a,b)}. Within this framework we examine the two classical approaches to estimation. The error of the empirical plug-in estimator is exactly a generalization gap, so generalization bounds transfer to it directly. The leave-one-out estimator, which recovers the Good--Turing estimator, is accurate for every mapping that is stable under the deletion of one sample point, including new structured examples such as neighborhoods of the sample and pierced sets. The main application of our framework is to error estimation for a predictor that combines a base classifier with memorized exceptions, a structure common in theory and in practice. For it, the test error is exactly the missing mass restricted to the error region of the base classifier, a region selected by the same sample. We formulate the general problem of \emph{adaptive missing mass estimation} to address such dependence and propose a natural hybrid estimator, the Good--Turing estimator restricted to the selected region. We show that the generalization of the base classifier alone does not guarantee the accuracy of this estimator, and derive two bounds on its error: the first one based on the VC dimension of possible error regions and another based on the mutual information of the selected region with the sample.

arXiv.title: MEMIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization
arXiv.abstract: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.

arXiv.title: Equation informed time reparametrization for physics informed neural networks
arXiv.abstract: Physics Informed Neural Networks offer a mesh-free approach to solving differential equations, but their application to time-dependent problems remains challenging, particularly when the governing dynamics involve widely different time scales. With collocation points spread uniformly in time, short intervals of rapid change are under resolved. This work introduces an equation informed time reparameterization framework that modifies the temporal coordinate used during PINN training based on the local dynamics of the governing equation. The proposed method follows a two stage procedure. First, a pilot PINN training provides an approximate solution, which is used to linearize the governing differential operator and estimate its local response to small perturbations. These responses are combined into a time-dependent rate function, large where the dynamics are fast, that defines a strictly increasing transformation from physical time to a new computational time coordinate. A second PINN is then trained on the transformed governing equation, with uniformly sampled collocation points in the new coordinate producing a nonuniform distribution in physical time. Different combination rules and spatial reduction strategies are considered. With the cost of the pilot training included, the method reduces the error by a factor of 4 to 29 relative to the best alternative method on the Kachanov Rabotnov creep-damage model near rupture, and by a factor of 5 to 16 relative to every alternative method on the Frank-Kamenetskii equation near blow up.

arXiv.title: Multi-Timescale Deliverability of Shared Hybrid Storage for AI Data Center Campuses
arXiv.abstract: Artificial intelligence data center (AIDC) campuses contain sustained power variations and subsecond power fluctuations, requiring both sufficient stored energy and fast response. A shared hybrid energy storage system (HESS) can mitigate aggregate AIDC power deviations, but interval-based schedules cannot capture the delay between commanded and delivered power at the campus point of common coupling (PCC). To this end, this paper proposes a multi-timescale scheduling model for mitigating AIDC power fluctuations with the shared HESS. First, it models electrical pooling at the campus bus and constrains the shared HESS to a single PCC injection. Second, a two-layer model passes five-minute scheduled power, energy state, and reserve capacity to a causal fast response model that distinguishes commanded power from delivered power. Case studies using the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) GenAI Power Profiles Dataset show reductions in both PCC and fast integral absolute error (IAE), while retaining most of the improvement available under ideal response.

arXiv.title: A Good-Vorticity Low-Regularity Integrator for the Inviscid Oldroyd--B System with Stress Diffusion
arXiv.abstract: We establish sharp convergence results for a sequential semi-implicit good-vorticity integrator for the two-dimensional inviscid Oldroyd--B system with stress diffusion on the torus. For exact solutions satisfying $u\in C_tB^{1+α}_{\infty,1}$ and $τ\in C_tB^α_{\infty,1}\cap L^1_tB^{2+α}_{\infty,1}$, $0\leα\le2$, we prove convergence in the critical norms $B^1_{\infty,1}\times B^0_{\infty,1}$, uniformly over the time nodes on every finite interval where these regularity assumptions hold, including the critical endpoint $α=0$. For $0<α\le2$, we obtain the rate $O(h^{α/2})$ without any additional time Hölder assumption, reaching first order at $α=2$. These algebraic exponents are optimal for this Eulerian scheme over the stated solution classes, as shown by fixed-data lower bounds in the case $a=b=0$ with nonzero velocity mean. For a fixed shear solution at critical regularity, we establish matching logarithmic upper and lower bounds on the numerical error, ruling out every positive algebraic convergence rate. We also prove that the gain of one stress derivative at the time nodes is optimal when the velocity is controlled in $B^1_{\infty,1}$, even for smooth initial stress.

arXiv.title: POST-MIMO: Partition-Oriented Semantic Transmission for MIMO Point Cloud Delivery
arXiv.comments: 6 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Accepted for IEEE GLOBECOM 2026
arXiv.abstract: Point clouds have become a fundamental data format for emerging three dimensional (3D) applications, while their wireless delivery remains challenging due to the large data volume and irregular geometric structure. Existing semantic point cloud transmission methods are mainly developed for single-input single-output systems, making them difficult to apply directly to multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. To address this issue, we propose a partition-oriented semantic transmission framework for MIMO (POST-MIMO) point cloud delivery. POST-MIMO partitions the input point cloud into spatially coherent blocks and aligns them with parallel MIMO streams. Based on this block-aligned representation, the transmitter employs a hierarchical encoder to capture both intra-block local geometry and inter-block global dependency, while the auxiliary side information is transmitted jointly to assist reconstruction. At the receiver, a progressive decoder reconstructs the block geometry in a progressive manner and restores the final point cloud with block-aware adjustment. Experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and lower computational resource consumption than representative reference schemes under the considered MIMO setting.

arXiv.title: Hawkeye: Reading Illegible Text with Vision Language Models
arXiv.abstract: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. These limitations are particularly apparent in egocentric applications like smart glasses, where text is often captured in noisy environments. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{BSTRB} (Blurry Scene Text Recognition Benchmark), a novel benchmark of 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations derived from 1,699 real-world video sequences. To support this, we present \textbf{Hawkeye}, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. We characterize the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.

arXiv.title: ReVEAL: Eliciting Role-Aware Latent Visual Evidence from MLLMs for Reasoning Video Object Segmentation
arXiv.abstract: Reasoning video object segmentation (ReVOS) requires segmenting the target specified by an implicit query throughout a video. Existing MLLM-based methods typically require costly cross-model alignment, tying MLLM training to a downstream segmentation model. We present ReVEAL, a decoupled thinking-with-video framework for ReVOS that elicits role-aware latent visual evidence from MLLM reasoning to directly guide segmentation. ReVEAL introduces Visual Evidence Tokens (VETs) into video reasoning to associate necessary visual regions or entities with target, background, or distractor roles, while a Dynamic Attention Layer Router adaptively aggregates VET-to-video attention across layers into role-specific grounding evidence. We train the MLLM to perform VET-augmented reasoning on our constructed ReVEAL-47K dataset, with a Contrastive Attention Grounding Loss as auxiliary supervision to apply role-specific constraints to VET attention and optimize layer routing for reliable latent grounding. At inference, ReVEAL identifies the target through this thinking-with-video process and fuses the resulting role-specific evidence to guide a frozen SAM2 in predicting target masks. Experiments on five benchmarks show that ReVEAL outperforms alignment-free baselines and remains competitive with alignment-based methods.

arXiv.title: PBSR: Pseudo-Burst Super-Resolution via Zero-Shot Novel View Synthesis
arXiv.comments: Accepted for publication in New Generation Computing. 17 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables
arXiv.journal-ref: New Generation Computing 44(4), 32 (2026)
arXiv.abstract: Burst super-resolution (BSR) achieves higher reconstruction fidelity than single-image super-resolution (SISR) by aggregating sub-pixel information from multiple frames. However, it requires a burst of frames captured under near-static conditions, and such frames are unavailable for single photographs or archival images. We propose Pseudo-Burst Super-Resolution (PBSR), which brings BSR-style reconstruction to the single-image input setting by synthesizing pseudo-burst frames via zero-shot novel view synthesis (NVS). PBSR first generates pseudo-burst frames with realistic parallax using a viewpoint sampling strategy calibrated to the pixel-shift distribution of real burst datasets. The frames are then processed by a BSR backbone equipped with a geometry-aware alignment module that reuses the NVS camera parameters and estimated depth. While the NVS stage is zero-shot, the backbone is fine-tuned with an artifact-aware adaptation so that it can exploit the synthesized frames despite their generative artifacts. Experiments on the BurstSR dataset show that PBSR consistently improves in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over the single-frame baseline with the same reconstruction backbone.

arXiv.title: SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
arXiv.abstract: Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored. We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching. Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model~(LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the \textit{MCSketch8K} dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement. The project page is: \href{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}.

arXiv.title: Yesterday's Code, Today's Dependencies: How Dependency Selection Shapes PHP Migration Benchmarks
arXiv.abstract: Migration benchmarks need projects whose tests pass before migration begins. Yet an old project can behave differently without any change to its code. Reinstalling it today may introduce newer libraries, changing both its initial test results and the failures observed during migration. We investigate this effect in PHP 7.4-to-8.3 migration. Using unchanged project source and saved package records, we compare two dependency policies. Modern selection allows all versions in the snapshot, while release-date selection allows only versions published by the project's release date. With Composer 2 fixed, release-date selection improves the PHP 7.4 pass rate by 7.1 pp across 3,660 releases. A separate comparison against committed locks shows that it also recovers recorded dependency versions more closely than modern selection. The choice matters after migration as well. Among projects that pass on PHP 7.4 under both policies, PHP 8.3 test outcomes differ in 15.0% of eligible pairs. We use a shared test runner and bypass Composer's platform check to isolate test behavior. The resulting candidate migration task sets overlap by only 58.5%. Most differences arise in Laravel projects, where older dependencies trigger deprecations that newer versions avoid. Targeted interventions show that removing these initial failures can restore passing tests or expose further incompatibilities. Thus, dependency selection changes not just whether an old project passes, but also which migration failures a benchmark can observe. Preserved locks provide the strongest available version reference; without them, release-date selection offers a historically grounded alternative. Migration benchmarks should make this choice explicit and report its effect on their results.

arXiv.title: Rome Wasn't Built in One Turn: Replay-Grounded Reward Signals for Long-Horizon Freeciv Agents
arXiv.abstract: Training language-model agents to play long-horizon strategy games is hard because deterministic feedback is sparse and often arrives only at the end of a game. In-game scores can offer dense signals, but they do not reliably predict future outcomes: in 8-68% of position pairs across eight strategy games, the higher-scoring position leads to the worse outcome. We term this phenomenon scoreboard traps. In Freeciv, an open-source turn-based empire-building game where several players manage units, cities, and diplomacy over hundreds of turns, we look into better reward signals for gameplay agents. To facilitate this, we build CivHarness, an open system that saves current game states, branches on different decisions, and replays the game to future turns to provide measurable long-horizon feedback from saved positions. We use CivHarness to train CivTelescope, an LLM Judge that predicts which one of two game positions will yield the better outcome. On scoreboard-trap pairs, CivTelescope is 1.3-2.0 times more accurate than off-the-shelf language models, and it generalizes to new game starts, later turns, and unseen rules. We then train a Freeciv gameplay agent with CivTelescope as a dense reward, and call this recipe CivMarshmallow. When used in the middle stage of the game where scoreboard traps are common, CivMarshmallow reaches an average training phase gain of 8.94 points, 77% more than the best baseline, the end-of-game reward. Over the full 120-turn game, CivMarshmallow uses a hybrid reward that starts from the scoreboard or the end-of-game reward and shifts to CivTelescope as the game advances; this hybrid reward scores highest among the rewards we compare.

arXiv.title: Input-dependent Neuromodulation Enhances Mixed-Signal Neuromorphic Hardware
arXiv.comments: 5 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to IEEE ISCAS 2027
arXiv.abstract: Gating mechanisms allow a fixed neural network to adapt its computation to the current input by dynamically modulating its effective parameters. In the brain, neuromodulation uses this principle to move neural circuits between dynamical regimes, and deep learning exploits input-dependent gating, e.g., in gated recurrent networks and self-attention. Input-dependent modulation has also recently been shown to improve spiking neural networks, with particularly strong benefits in small, parameter-limited ones. This makes neuromodulation especially promising for neuromorphic processors at the edge, where area, memory and energy budgets constrain network size, while circuit physics limits parameter precision. Here we demonstrate input-dependent, within-trial neuromodulation of a spiking recurrent neural network on a mixed-signal neuromorphic processor. An off-chip modulator reads the on-chip network's input and activity and adjusts its population-level gains while the chip's analog circuits compute with the physics of the silicon. Neuromodulation raises binary spoken-digit classification accuracy by $+17.3 \pm 10.4$ percentage points, tested across five hardware network instantiations.

arXiv.title: From 1D Benchmarks to Complex 3D Geometries: Can Agents Reliably Specify Problems for Automated PDE Simulation?
arXiv.abstract: Turning an engineering request into a simulation requires consistent geometry, physics, boundary conditions, and numerical settings. Recent agent-assisted systems automate simulation setup, but successful execution alone does not establish whether the specification preserves the intended problem or correctly handles missing information. We study whether agents can reliably construct complete executable JSON specifications for automated geometry creation, meshing, PDE solving, and result export. Our workflow combines model extraction with deterministic scientific and capability checks, explicit clarification, and validated local patches that preserve unrelated accepted fields. We evaluate specification correctness, execution completion, and numerical verification separately. On 120 template-related requests, the full workflow achieves 98.3% correct first-turn specification and decision outcomes, compared with 92.5% for schema-assisted single shot and 82.5% for model-only: gains of 5.8 and 15.8 percentage points, respectively. It makes no false-ready decisions among the 42 requests requiring clarification or rejection. Component ablations identify contributions from scientific checks and conditional repair. Separate downstream studies cover 1D, 2D, and 3D steady and unsteady, linear and nonlinear problems, including flow and elasticity with complex three-dimensional wing geometries. A 30-case gallery demonstrates automated execution from retained JSON specifications, while 9 of 12 selected live user-to-results tests achieve joint specification, execution, export, and numerical-reference success (75.0%). These results support traceable, engineer-reviewed simulation assistance within the tested scope, while fresh-response regressions identify consistency as a priority for further improvement.

arXiv.title: Coarse-Graining Optimal Transport for Rollout-Free Post-Training of Flow Matching
arXiv.abstract: Flow matching depends critically on the coupling used to pair source and target samples. Optimal transport (OT) couplings can reduce velocity conflict and straighten trajectories; but, in practice, challenges remain: the source comes from a continuous distribution, only a finite number of target samples data are accessible, and the neural network has finite capacity. For these reasons, making the coupling more OT-like may not consistently improve sampling quality, in particular in the low number-of-function-evaluation (NFE) regime. Motivated by this, we introduce ReCouple, a controllable framework that constructs coarse-grained OT couplings, to better understand rollout-free OT-based post-training. We also consider extensions of this basic framework: ReCouple+ extends this toward the continuous-source setting by increasing source resolution, converging to semi-discrete OT in the appropriate limit; and ReCouple++ further adds spatial regularization, motivated by the observation that straight trajectories need not correspond to spatially simple velocity fields. Empirical validation demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods, and it reveals an NFE-dependent interplay between coupling optimality, neural realizability, and generation quality.

arXiv.title: ANGLER: Verifier-Grounded Benchmarking with an Adaptive Attacker for Web Agents
arXiv.abstract: Web agents are increasingly deployed to complete tasks autonomously on real websites, where adversarially injected content can induce them to perform unauthorized actions. Existing evaluations primarily use fixed attacks or focus on a single attack type, and evaluate attacks at the text level rather than through real state changes, thus underestimating how vulnerable agents are to diverse attacks. To address the gap, we introduce REEF, a benchmark of red-teaming executable environments with faithful verification for measuring the security vulnerabilities of web agents. REEF covers 9 verifier-grounded websites spanning travel, commerce, productivity, media, and communication, and pairs every authentic benign task with a malicious objective delivered through 5 attack types at both the user and the environment level. REEF's state-based verifiers provide the execution feedback that drives ANGLER, an adaptive near-miss-guided lure evolution framework for red-teaming. Rather than evaluating a fixed attack set, ANGLER uses outcomes from prior rollouts to guide LLM-based attack mutation and candidate selection, prioritizing near-miss seeds during refinement. Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER achieves an end-to-end attack success rate (ASR) of 20.36%, compared with 15.24% for the non-adaptive setting. Compared with attack-free execution on the same benign tasks, attacks generated by ANGLER reduce benign task success rate (BSR) from 61.9% to 44.4%.

arXiv.title: Architectural Debt Enforcement under Incomplete Observation: A Controlled Study of Ratchets and Evidence Qualification
arXiv.abstract: Architectural debt gates must distinguish an allowed change from an incompletely observed one. We study a decision contract separating observation qualification, prohibited relation identity, inherited debt and authorized baseline updates. Across 240 fixed files from four repositories, the current observer and programmatic reference jointly qualify 166 files (69.17%), all with exact reference-relative edge agreement; 74 remain reference-UNKNOWN. Coverage varies from 13/60 to 59/60 by repository. On 480 constructed state scenarios sharing 60 source anchors, both the candidate ratchet and mature dependency-cruiser baseline match every expected outcome, whereas static and count-only baselines match 420 and 360. These results do not establish candidate superiority. Preserved failures include nine additional false-PASS probes and 120 unqualified full-tree timing attempts. A subsequent generic binding layer rejects 54 specified mismatches, accepts 54 current controls and permits legal repetition. Two bounded package scopes support 40 scenarios and 48 fresh-process functional checks; their costs remain tied to the measured implementations. Diagnostics explain residual uncertainty through type/runtime relations, installation context and generated-artifact provenance. TypeScript 5.9.3 and 6.0.2 yield identical outputs on ten paired emission witnesses, but neither that agreement nor verified release provenance changes the frozen UNKNOWN labels. The contribution is a controlled account of evidence-qualified enforcement and its limits, not language completeness, natural maintenance effectiveness or a new shrinking-baseline algorithm.

arXiv.title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning
arXiv.comments: 9 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for publication at the 4th International Conference on Federated Learning Technologies and Applications (FLTA 2026). The final version will appear in the conference proceedings published by IEEE
arXiv.abstract: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.

arXiv.title: SciGraphSelect: Auditable Scientific Data Selection through Knowledge--Reasoning Graphs
arXiv.comments: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: AI4Science
arXiv.abstract: Scientific data selection is typically driven by relevance or utility scores, providing limited insight into why a document is retained. We introduce SciGraphSelect, a reference-grounded framework for auditable scientific data selection. SciGraphSelect organizes domain-specific knowledge, reusable reasoning operations, and reference-attested relations into a typed knowledge--reasoning graph, then scores candidate documents using concept coverage, relation and path co-support, and directional alignment. To avoid over-interpreting document embeddings, rich relational structure is preserved on the reference side while candidate-side evidence is treated conservatively without assuming relation entailment. By exposing the reference-grounded evidence behind each selection, SciGraphSelect brings traceability to the upstream construction of scientific training corpora and complements downstream scientific verification.

arXiv.title: Estimation of Quantum Umlaut Information
arXiv.abstract: Quantifying correlations is important for understanding how quantum states and channels support information processing. Quantum umlaut information $U$ connects such correlations to reliability in hypothesis testing and certain communication settings, but its known formulas require classical descriptions of the underlying states. To estimate correlations without these descriptions, we introduce measured quantum umlaut information $U^M$ by replacing Umegaki relative entropy with measured relative entropy. Its variational formulation leads to a quantum generative adversarial framework for estimating $U^M$ from measurement statistics of unknown bipartite states and classical-quantum channels. This framework optimizes reference states and measurements without reconstructing the target states or channel outputs. For classical-quantum channels, it also optimizes the input probabilities. We further analyze the relation between $U^M$ and $U$, deriving a state-dependent gap bound and characterizing equality for full-rank bipartite states. Numerical simulations show trained estimates close on average to independently computed numerical references for $U^M$ across the tested states and channels. These estimates could help assess how well quantum memories preserve correlations and how noise or drift affects input-output dependence in quantum transmitters and state-preparation devices.

arXiv.title: Truthful and Admissible Principal--Agent Testing with Nuisance Parameters
arXiv.abstract: Statistical contracts reward experimenters according to the evidence produced by a costly study, so the reward rule influences both who participates and what they report. Principal--agent testing theory explains how to prevent ineffective proposals from being profitable. We ask when such contracts can also elicit honest parameter reports if the decision concerns a mean effect but the variance or distributional shape is unknown. Under risk neutrality and a fixed participation cost, we construct menus of e-values --- nonnegative normalized rewards with expected value at most one under every null --- such that (i) agents who know they are null have no incentive to participate, (ii) every alternative type earns positive expected profit and is thus incentivized to participate, (iii) truthful reporting uniquely maximizes expected their reward, (iv) and each contract is admissible: its payouts cannot be pointwise improved while retaining null validity. For Gaussian observations, we treat separately agents who know both mean and variance and agents who know only their mean; in the latter case, truthfulness holds at every variance without requiring a nuisance prior. Multi-sample extensions preserve these incentives and can reward accumulating evidence. Beyond Gaussian models, we show that two independent nonnegative observations suffice to elicit any finite mean above a positive null threshold, without any further distributional knowledge, but one observation cannot combine strict mean elicitation with individual admissibility on this class. Finally, we distinguish the existence of useful tests from the identification needed for truthful contracts. Boundedness is not required, and finitely many null constraints do not by themselves guarantee admissible elicitation.

arXiv.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
arXiv.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

arXiv.title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
arXiv.abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

arXiv.title: Assortativity and the Distribution of Spectral Gaps in Directed Networks
arXiv.abstract: This paper studies how the distribution of spectral gaps of a weighted directed network varies with its assortativity. We prove that the sum of the distances of each of the eigenvalues from the Perron root along the real axis, which we call the `spectral depth', decreases as the network is rewired to be less assortative. The result is conditional on the network's Perron vectors ordering the rewired vertices in the same way as their strengths do. We also develop a method to determine whether a particular spectral gap contracts or expands under a rewiring that changes the network's assortativity. It turns out that the direction of any one gap depends on far more than the network's assortativity. In computational experiments on heavy-tailed networks, disassortative rewiring lowers the spectral depth by about two fifths, contracts most strongly the gaps in the middle of the spectrum, and collapses a growing part of the spectrum to zero. The experiments also show that a sequence of disassortative rewirings tends to narrow the first spectral gap, while a sequence of assortative rewirings widens it.

arXiv.title: Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards: Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer
arXiv.abstract: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.

arXiv.title: Toward Low-Burden Image-Based Dietary Assessment Through Human-AI Collaborative Correction
arXiv.abstract: Image-based dietary assessment can automate initial food logging, but meal photographs often leave food identity, hidden ingredients, preparation, and portion uncertain, making correction a recurring part of use. We introduce Human-AI Collaborative Correction, which reframes correction as communicate intent $\rightarrow$ regenerate $\rightarrow$ verify: users express what should change through text, voice, or guided clarification, the AI regenerates the linked dietary record, and users verify the result. In a within-participant study with 30 participants, compared with conventional Manual Search-and-Edit Correction, collaborative correction was associated with lower workload (Raw TLX: 35.83 vs. 55.00; p < .001), 21.0% lower recorded usage time, 51.1% fewer recorded clicks, and more favorable user-experience ratings; 90.0% preferred it overall. An exploratory nutrient analysis also found lower energy MAE. These findings support intent-driven regeneration as a promising interaction pattern for reducing correction burden while preserving user verification and making image-based dietary tracking easier to sustain.

arXiv.title: Subliminal Reinforcement Learning: traits travel through a judge's scores
arXiv.comments: 37 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, 2 Extended Data figures, 6 Extended Data tables; Supplementary Information included. Code and data: https://github.com/kkt94/subliminal-rl
arXiv.abstract: Subliminal learning, the transfer of a model's trait through data with no semantic trace of it, has been shown for students trained on a teacher's text. Post-training relies on group relative policy optimization with a language-model judge, where the student learns only from its own outputs and one judge's scores. We show this suffices: a student writes invented syllables or numbers, a judge made to prefer one animal scores them, and the student's preference moves toward that animal relative to a run whose judge prefers another. Of 48 design cells, two fail the validity gate and 17 establish the trait at 5% false-discovery rate, numbers-only cells included; elsewhere, our account gives the reason. Removing only the reward difference between judges removes transfer. We establish the principle as a chain of four stages: the trait must show in the judge's scores, favour strings that move the student, accumulate and reach the answers. Judges with the same preference built from other data, or on another model, place it on other strings, and transfer is not detected. Carried unchanged to AI-safety dispositions, the chain holds: undesirable dispositions reach the student's answers, and stages measured before training anticipate where, helping to prevent part of this risk.

arXiv.title: Scaled-Gradient Hard Thresholding Algorithms for Sparse Signal Recovery
arXiv.abstract: Thresholding methods provide a simple iterative framework for sparse signal recovery by combining a search direction with a thresholding operation. Gradient-based search directions are computationally efficient because they require only first-order information for the error metric. We incorporate componentwise gradient scaling into this framework by preserving large-magnitude components and attenuating the remaining components of the gradient of error metric. Combining this strategy with hard thresholding yields scaled-gradient hard thresholding (SGHT) and its pursuit variant SGHTP. Under suitable restricted isometry conditions, we establish recovery error bounds for both methods that account for measurement noise and deviations from exact sparsity. Numerical experiments indicate that SGHTP achieves recovery performance comparable to established pursuit methods on the tested ECG signals.

arXiv.title: rl_rob: A transparent, from-scratch Python library for teaching reinforcement learning from tabular methods to deep policy gradients
arXiv.abstract: rl_rob is an open-source Python library for teaching reinforcement learning. It implements the arc of a modern course, from tabular temporal-difference learning through linear function approximation to deep value-based and policy-gradient methods, with every algorithm written from first principles so that its update rule is visible in a few lines of code. All agents share one interface, so learners can compare methods directly across stages and trace a deep reinforcement learning update from the temporal-difference error to the weight change. The library supports teaching and assessment in which students implement, modify and explain update rules, rather than only produce working code.

arXiv.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
arXiv.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

arXiv.title: Feature-preserving interface reconstruction using piecewise circles and cusps
arXiv.comments: 55 pages, 30 figures. Code and benchmark data: https://github.com/jerrywliu/interface-reconstruction/releases/tag/jcp-submission-2026-10-22-r1
arXiv.abstract: We present a geometric interface reconstruction method for Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) simulations that captures both curved interfaces and sharp features using only volume fraction data. We represent interfaces with linear facets, circular arcs, and corner facets formed by two lines or arcs joined within a single cell. We first propagate local orientation constraints through a graph and merge cells to resolve ambiguities, treating topological consistency as a first-class constraint. An optional conservative refinement improves $C^0$ continuity while preserving local volume constraints. Users can independently enable circular facets, corner facets, cell merging, and continuity refinement to balance accuracy and computational cost. In its simplest configuration, our method provides a fast local line-fitting scheme competitive with state-of-the-art PLIC methods. On standard static benchmarks, the full configuration reconstructs identifiable lines, circles, and sufficiently resolved corners to numerical precision on coarse, perturbed Cartesian meshes. On varying-curvature interfaces, it achieves third-order convergence in facet-gap error and approximately first-order convergence in curvature error. These results demonstrate global volume conservation and accurate reconstruction of curved and corner features.

arXiv.title: Erase the Injected Region: Multimodal Prompt-Injection Defense with On-Policy Self-Distillation
arXiv.abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

arXiv.title: SERIAL-7: Deriving, Realizing, and Preserving Machine-Verifiable Outputs Across Representations
arXiv.comments: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding
arXiv.abstract: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs consumed by programs and downstream systems, where semantic correctness alone does not guarantee reliable execution.
