Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. We evaluate two domain-specific language models, BioBERT (108M parameters) and BioMistral (7B parameters), for phase-level outcome prediction on the TOP benchmark (12,477 trials), representing each trial as text built from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields. We compare fine-tuning (full fine-tuning for BioBERT, low-rank adaptation for BioMistral) with probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings. On the held-out test set of each phase, all four language-model variants achieved higher ROC-AUC (0.613--0.772) and PR-AUC (0.649--0.901) than the published HINT results, corresponding to relative PR-AUC gains of 10--20\%. F1 differences were small and mixed, and no model, including HINT, clearly exceeded the F1 of a trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial. Under the configurations tested, probing performed comparably to fine-tuning: fine-tuned models scored highest on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC in Phases I and II, and frozen BioMistral embeddings in Phase III (ROC-AUC 0.772; PR-AUC 0.901), although most differences between variants were below 0.03 and were not tested for significance. These results suggest that pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal relevant to trial outcome, and that probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.

arXiv.title: Hierarchical Residuals: A Minimalist Decoupling of Residual Width from Compute Width
arXiv.abstract: Residual connections underpin Transformers, but they implicitly tie the residual width carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. We introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), a minimalist architectural change that decouples these dimensions, widening the residual state while keeping per-layer compute width fixed. HiRes groups layers into blocks: standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers operate inside each block, while a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connects blocks. Learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, leaving individual Transformer layers unchanged. Across different model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold improvement in FLOPs efficiency. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. HiRes is also competitive with other residual expansion methods such as VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O costs. Built from only dense projections and normalizations, it requires neither specialized kernels nor infrastructure-level optimizations. HiRes thus exposes residual width as a practical scaling variable using only standard operators.

arXiv.title: Simple Features Beat Most AI Control Monitors
arXiv.comments: 19 pages (5-page main body plus appendix), 7 figures, 10 tables. Accepted at the EvoRobust workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code and data: https://github.com/ShubsDS/authorship-not-sabotage
arXiv.abstract: AI control relies on monitors to catch a capable model that sabotages its work. These monitors are evaluated on their ability to differentiate honest from backdoored code. We show that on a standard evaluation dataset, simple features beat most monitors without ever running the code, outranking 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors. The dataset gives its labels away in two ways. People wrote the honest solutions and older language models the backdoors, so the style of the code reveals the class. Additionally, problems that LLMs can backdoor have different characteristics, so basic facts about the problem reveal it too. Swapping one class at a time for code by Claude Sonnet 5 shows that these features reward a contrast between authors, since human code against Sonnet 5's backdoors is easier to separate than the original pairs, 0.95 against 0.79. One in seven backdoors in the standard test set fails our validity checks, which distorts comparisons between attackers. A Sonnet 5 monitor appears to catch 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified. We do not show that published monitors rely on these shortcuts, but our findings suggest that a high score on such a dataset is not by itself evidence of sabotage detection. We release the rebuilt dataset and checks.

arXiv.title: A Fully Polynomial Randomized Approximation Scheme for Hypergraph Unreliability
arXiv.abstract: We give a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for all-terminal unreliability in explicitly represented undirected hypergraphs of arbitrary rank. The algorithm estimates the probability that independent hyperedge failures disconnect the hypergraph, allowing a different rational failure probability for every edge. For a common failure probability, this improves the quasi-polynomial approximation schemes of Cen, Li, and Panigrahi to polynomial time and answers the polynomial-time approximation question reiterated in their subsequent work on graphs. The construction turns their representative-survival bound into an importance sampler whose relative second moment is bounded solely in terms of the number of vertices. We protect one randomly chosen representative pair during contraction, correct the path likelihood, and divide by the number of pairs surviving at the end. The resulting unbiased estimator has relative second moment at most $\binom n2$, even when unreliability is exponentially small. A minimum-cut normalization makes this estimator implementable with polynomially bounded precision: the residual likelihood becomes a survival probability in an auxiliary absorbing process, which admits rational discretization with a fixed random-bit budget. Logarithmic rate rounding and an exact weighted minimum cut extend the construction to unequal rational failure probabilities. The algorithm's worst-case running time and random-bit usage are polynomial in the input length, the inverse relative error, and $\log(1/δ)$ for confidence $1-δ$.

arXiv.title: Numerical analysis of linear finite element methods for the Gross--Pitaevskii eigenvalue problem
arXiv.abstract: In this paper, we analyze the standard and the mass-lumped linear finite element methods for the Gross--Pitaevskii eigenvalue problem. For the standard method, we give a new proof of the uniqueness of the discrete ground state up to sign for sufficiently small mesh sizes, which only requires the $H^1$-convergence of the discrete ground states. For both methods, we establish optimal convergence rates in the $L^p$- and $W^{1,p}$-norms for $1 \le p < \infty$. Under additional regularity assumptions on the potential, we further obtain an optimal convergence rate in the $W^{1,\infty}$-norm and an almost optimal convergence rate, up to a logarithmic factor, in the $L^\infty$-norm. Moreover, we prove that the discrete ground states superconverge to the Ritz projection of the exact ground state in the $W^{1,p}$-seminorm. The analysis is based on a perturbation argument. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical results.

arXiv.title: UpLoop: Training Looped Transformers via Upcycling at No Extra Pretraining Compute
arXiv.abstract: Looped language models can strengthen reasoning through repeated computation with shared weights, increasing execution depth without adding independent parameters. However, each additional pass increases training floating-point operations (FLOPs), making these gains more expensive to obtain. To address this cost, we propose UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that uses upcycling to train looped Transformers while exactly matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, total training tokens, and training FLOPs. Specifically, UpLoop begins with a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training. Experiments across model scales show improvements in language modeling and downstream performance, with the average score across 22 downstream tasks increasing from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters. These gains also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.

arXiv.title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
arXiv.abstract: In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. To connect the circuit's Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with $303$ shots per sample against a high-shot reference of $1.6\times10^{6}$, about $5300\times$ fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.

arXiv.title: Catalytic space-efficient algorithms for Distance and Determinant
arXiv.abstract: Catalytic computation reuses potentially large but in-use space (or catalytic space) which must be restored to its initial contents while the clean space is small. This allows all problems in $\mathsf{NL}$ and even larger classes to be in catalytic logspace [Buhrman et al, STOC2014]. In [Chmel et al, CCC2026] the catalytic space for reachability was restricted to sublinear space (specifically, $n \big/ 2^{θ(\sqrt{\log n})}$ space) while remaining in polynomial time. This matches the non-catalytic bounds from [Barnes et al, SICOMP1998]. We extend the reachability bound to shortest distance, proving a simultaneous sublinear catalytic space and polynomial time bound (henceforth called, sublinear $\mathsf{CLP}$). This is the first simultaneous sublinear space and polynomial time bound for distance even without the catalytic discipline. Moreover, our bound works even for polynomially weighted graphs. Along the way we prove simultaneous near linear catalytic space ($\mathcal{O}(n\log^{O(1)}{n})$) and polynomial time bounds for the determinant. We also show some applications to planar matching problems. Our starting point was catalytic computation of reachability in directed graphs by [Cook-Pyne, ITCS2026]. [Edenhofer, arXiv:2602.21088] used it to give a tradeoff between catalytic and non-catalytic space, while [Chmel et al, CCC2026] compress the graph to a smaller graph preserving $s,t$-reachability to achieve a smaller space bound. All three can be modified to yield an algorithm for unweighted distance. Our contribution is to define an approximation to the walk polynomial in weighted graphs that allows us to infer weighted $s,t$-distance in sublinear $\mathsf{CLP}$. We do so by non-trivially combining elements from each of the above three papers.

arXiv.title: When Architectural Spaces Start to Act
arXiv.abstract: Architectural spaces are increasingly gaining robotic capabilities. Architectural robots such as robotic partitions, ceilings, furniture, facades, and other spatial components can autonomously move and reconfigure in response to occupants' needs and activities. Yet, when architectural robots start shaping the spatial conditions in which people continuously live, work, and interact, we may begin to experience the architectural space itself as robotic. What does this shift mean for how we inhabit such spaces? Drawing on our previous studies, I reflect on how architectural robots interact with people not only through their motions, but also through the spatial configurations that persist after those motions stop; how their actions may benefit some occupants while disadvantaging others; and how multiple robots may together make a whole architectural space appear to act. I argue that as computation gains the capacity to physically reconfigure our environments, interaction extends beyond the moment of computational action into the spatial conditions that people continue to inhabit. Understanding robotic architecture therefore requires us to look beyond short-term human-robot interaction and toward how people inhabit, negotiate, and maintain control over spaces that can autonomously reconfigure.

arXiv.title: SAR-TS-BERT: Physics-Guided Self-Supervised Pre-Training With Polarimetric Features for SAR Time-Series Crop Classification
arXiv.comments: 18 pages, 13 figures, 18 tables. Jieqiu Wang and Yuhan Zhang contributed equally to this work
arXiv.abstract: Multitemporal synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery provides continuous, cloud-free observations of crop phenology for agricultural monitoring in cloudy and rainy regions, yet high-accuracy classification typically requires extensive labeled samples. Although self-supervised pre-training mitigates label dependency in remote sensing, existing frameworks primarily target optical imagery or generic spatial SAR scenes, underutilizing temporal backscatter dynamics and polarimetric scattering mechanisms. We propose SAR-TS-BERT, a physics-guided BERT-style self-supervised pre-training framework for SAR time-series crop classification. SAR-TS-BERT integrates backscatter intensities and polarimetric ratio features (VV, VH, and VV/VH) with dual-polarimetric Cloude-Pottier decomposition parameters ($H/α/A$) into a six-band input representation through two core designs: 1) a physics-guided span masking strategy (SpanPhysics) that adaptively selects contiguous masked spans based on temporal backscatter change rates to prioritize key phenological transitions; and 2) a dual-branch cross-modal fusion encoder that models backscatter and polarimetric decomposition features through separate Transformer branches followed by bidirectional cross-attention fusion. On independent test sets in Estonia (EuroCropsML) and the USA (California CDL), SAR-TS-BERT achieves overall accuracies (OAs) of 96.78% and 87.29%, respectively, and attains a mean monthly OA of 99.37% on Chongming Island, Shanghai. On the Estonia benchmark, pre-training improves OA and Macro F1 by 1.17 and 1.59 percentage points over training from scratch under full supervision, and by 2.58 and 5.19 percentage points using only 1% labeled data. Incorporating SAR scattering physics into temporal self-supervised pre-training effectively enhances crop classification accuracy, parcel-level mapping consistency, and few-shot transferability.

arXiv.title: From Training Exposure to Membership Evidence: A Controlled Study of OLMo 2
arXiv.abstract: Whether a language model was trained on a document matters for copyright, privacy, and benchmark contamination. Yet most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive. We re-ran OLMo 2 1B's official 50-billion-token mid-training stage, replacing selected training chunks with documents from 7,814 pairs matched on domain and difficulty. For each pair, a coin flip determined which document was inserted and which was held out. The run released by the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from the same seed saw identical data everywhere else and serves as the counterfactual. One exposure raises a previously unseen document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Using the counterfactual as reference, the reference ratio has an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.767 but, with one threshold across domains, catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate (FPR). In contrast, 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection, given same-domain non-members and a close reference. A reference trained with another seed recovers 92% of the counterfactual's AUC advantage over chance, whereas reference-free attacks stay within 0.07 of chance when pooled over domains. The full official post-training recipe, re-run on both models, leaves 89% of the average effect. Even with a closely matched reference, substantial document-level variability limits individual membership inference. We will release the checkpoints, per-token log-probabilities, and the evaluation documents; the code is available at https://github.com/ali-bana/OLMo-Twin.

arXiv.title: Leakage-Controlled Structure-Preserving Augmentation and Template-Aware Evaluation for Bangla Symptom-Based Disease Prediction
arXiv.abstract: Bangla symptom-based disease prediction is commonly evaluated on a small, imbalanced structured benchmark containing many profiles that differ by only one or two symptoms. We test whether train-only asymmetric Bernoulli perturbation improves classification using 725 unique profiles spanning 85 diseases and 172 binary symptoms. Experiments use ten repeated real-profile holdouts and parent-grouped inner cross-validation. The 2 x 2 design separates augmentation from hyperparameter tuning, with exact duplication, random oversampling, class weighting, and SMOTEN as balancing controls. For Bernoulli Naive Bayes (BNB), the gain over tuned raw training does not withstand Holm correction, although BNB attains the highest mean accuracy (97.50%). The boosted-tree models benefit substantially: XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost improve by 18.10, 28.45, and 10.09 percentage points, respectively. A Hamming-distance audit places 91.0% of standard held-out profiles within one symptom bit of the training data. Accuracy decreases on a same-disease 1-bit-purged challenge; nevertheless, XGBoost and LightGBM retain large augmentation gains. We also evaluate robustness to missing and spurious symptoms and the faithfulness of BNB explanations. Overall, Bernoulli perturbation is useful for some model families, but benchmark accuracy should be interpreted together with template proximity.

arXiv.title: Maximum edge overlap between independent random regular graphs
arXiv.abstract: Optimising the vertex correspondence can substantially increase the number of edges shared by two independent realisations of the same random graph. We quantify this phenomenon for uniformly random $d$-regular graphs and derive corresponding results for their edge-based graph edit distance. For every fixed $d\geq 3$, we show that the maximum overlap is $n+Θ_{\mathbb P}(n/\log n)$, where the leading term $n$ arises from Hamiltonicity, while the surplus captures the optimal order of the excess beyond it. We establish explicit upper and lower bounds on the surplus. The upper bound is obtained by counting common cores of minimum degree at least two, while the lower bound is established using spanning factors consisting of cycles of the same logarithmic length. For the special case $d=2$, we show that the maximum overlap is $n-(1+o_{\mathbb P}(1))\log n$. The additional overlap achievable is also studied by rotating aligned Hamilton cycles, using a contiguity argument. As a by-product, we determine the asymptotic maximum overlap between unions of independent random perfect matchings under cyclic shifts.

arXiv.title: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design
arXiv.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA sequences for targeted gene-expression control is an important challenge. Recent approaches frame this task as property-conditioned generation, where diffusion models trained on natural sequences are guided toward high predicted activity through reward-based fine-tuning or sampling-time guidance. We show that single-reward evaluation can obscure reward-hacking behavior. By decomposing evaluation into property, novelty, and plausibility, we identify an empirically underexplored region of the evaluation space in which all three objectives are satisfied, but no existing baseline succeeds. We postulate that this gap arises because prior methods treat guidance primarily as a matter of magnitude. In regulatory DNA, however, sequence grammar is spatially nonuniform: motif positions are sensitive to perturbation, while background regions allow more exploration. We therefore propose LOCOGEN by reformulating guidance as a problem of locality. LOCOGEN learns an invariant motif mask through sequence-level invariance learning to protect motif positions, while applying OOD damping only to background positions. It operates at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone, without retraining the backbone. Across HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH, LOCOGEN reaches this previously underexplored region of the property-novelty-plausibility space. Code is available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/LocoGen.

arXiv.title: Search When Needed, Proceed When Reliable: Metacognitive Reliability Supervision for Efficient Agentic Search
arXiv.abstract: Efficient agentic search requires large language models (LLMs) to determine whether they can reliably proceed with their current knowledge or need additional external evidence. Supervision based on final-answer correctness or trajectory-level feedback evaluates realized trajectory performance. However, observed trajectory performance is jointly shaped by stochastic generation, retrieval quality, and downstream reasoning. Such signals therefore provide only indirect evidence of how reliable the current decision state was and how retrieved evidence changed its reliability. An effective reward should encourage search when external information is needed and favor searches that contribute to the answer. To this end, we propose a metacognitive framework for training LLMs to make search decisions based on the reliability of their intermediate reasoning states. Our framework estimates the reliability of local conclusions to distinguish whether the current information supports proceeding without search from how much retrieved evidence improves that reliability. The current-state reliability score assesses whether the model can proceed without search. The search-action score measures how retrieved evidence changes estimated reliability. Together, these scores define a reliability-aware process reward for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), providing finer-grained supervision for search and no-search behavior. Experiments across seven question-answering benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off than strong agentic-search baselines. Our code and model checkpoints will be open-sourced.

arXiv.title: Task Vectors Can Be Linearly Decomposed into Interpretable and Controllable Components
arXiv.abstract: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.

arXiv.title: Feasibility of Common-Stream-Only Sensing in ZF-RSMA with Imperfect CSIT
arXiv.comments: Accepted at IEEE GLOBECOM 2026. 6 pages, 5 figures
arXiv.abstract: Reusing the Rate-Splitting Multiple Access (RSMA) common stream for sensing eliminates dedicated probing signals in Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC), but creates a feasibility bottleneck: the common-power fraction must simultaneously support common decoding, private decoding, and target detection. This paper investigates this tradeoff in downlink zero-forcing RSMA with imperfect channel state information at the transmitter (CSIT) and imperfect successive interference cancellation (SIC). With the common beam fixed over a sensing dwell through sensing geometry, the common-power fraction becomes the sole design variable. We prove that the communication-feasible set is either a closed interval or empty. Analytical outage expressions localize these endpoints, revealing a high-signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) floor-ceiling effect: common decoding dictates a common-power floor, while imperfect CSIT and SIC impose a private-decoding ceiling. For sensing, the conditional detection constraint is affine, preserving the interval structure. A geometry-matched common beam ensures monotonic detection improvement, reducing joint-feasibility check to the communication-feasible upper endpoint. Simulations validate our analysis, identifying regimes where common-stream-only sensing is viable.

arXiv.title: Do LLMs Know When They Are Wrong About Molecules? In-Context Property Prediction with Self-Reported Uncertainty
arXiv.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used in many domains, but molecular property prediction with them is still little explored. In this work we evaluate the capability of 7 frontier LLMs to predict molecular properties together with a self-reported uncertainty from in-context examples, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. We use 4 datasets and screen each for contamination of the training data of the LLMs: three are clean, and the fourth, ESOL, is memorised by most of the models and serves as a comparison. On the clean datasets every LLM improves with the context, at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline. The requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little. The self-reported uncertainty ranks the prediction errors weakly, with Spearman rank correlations of up to 0.46, about the level reached by the uncertainties of the baselines. Combining uncertainty and prediction, on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes; on BACE and antiviral, and on lipophilicity at large context sizes, the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline. On the contaminated ESOL dataset the LLMs show no improvement with the context size, as expected for a memorised dataset, and their stated uncertainty is smaller on the molecules whose value they recall.

arXiv.title: $W^{1,p}$ error estimates of an IPDG and a class of HDG methods for the Poisson problem on convex polyhedral domains
arXiv.abstract: This paper analyzes a symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin (IPDG) method, a hybrid mixed DG method, and two representative hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) methods for the Poisson problem on convex polyhedral domains. For any fixed $ε\in (0,\frac{1}{2})$, we first derive optimal discrete $W^{1,p}$ error estimates for $2\leq p<\frac{1}ε$ by combining the interface Green's functions developed in \cite{lq2026} with the Fubini-type weighted estimates established in this paper. These error estimates lead to discrete $W^{1,q}$-$W^{1,p}$ inf-sup stability for $2\leq q<\frac{1}ε$, where $q$ is the conjugate number of $p$ such that $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1$. Using this stability result and a suitably constructed dual problem, we extend the optimal error estimates to $\frac{1}{1-ε}<p<2$ and subsequently establish the corresponding inf-sup stability for $\frac{1}{1-ε}< q<2$. Thus, both optimal discrete $W^{1,p}$ error estimates and discrete $W^{1,q}$-$W^{1,p}$ inf-sup stability hold throughout the range $\frac{1}{1-ε}<p<\frac{1}ε$, with $q=p/(p-1)$. Note that all of the aforementioned results are free of logarithmic factors and also hold on polyhedral meshes (except for the hybrid mixed DG method). Compared with the conforming finite element method (FEM), establishing such error estimates and inf-sup stability results for DG methods on convex polyhedral domains is more delicate because their analysis involves mesh-dependent norms. Consequently, the operator interpolation theory employed for conforming FEMs cannot be directly applied to DG methods. Finally, a numerical example is presented to illustrate the theoretical results.

arXiv.title: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication
arXiv.abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.

arXiv.title: Higher-Order Kinematic Derivatives for Aspect-Preserving Real-Time Numerical Inverse Kinematics
arXiv.abstract: This paper leverages the higher-order kinematic derivatives of serial robots to achieve efficient, aspect-preserving real-time inverse kinematics. First, a family of higher-order solvers is derived, with a necessary orientation-error correction map, yielding the QuIK4 and QuIK5 methods with fourth- and fifth-order convergence. Second, an aspect-preserving step limiter extrapolates the Jacobian determinant along the step to predict and avoid singularities, shortening steps only when they head toward a singularity rather than when the current iterate is ill-conditioned. Third, a Hermite-interpolation certifier verifies the aspect of each answer, and a certified restart algorithm recovers failures from proven same-aspect seeds. The proposed methods are shown to outperform prior methods, reducing failures by up to four orders of magnitude and nearly eliminating aspect switching at tracking-level errors. A C++ library is released with ROS 2 integration.

arXiv.title: Multimodal In-Context Learning with Explicit Rule Induction
arXiv.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal in-context learning (MICL) arises from tasks that are ill-defined without context and require uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations. Existing methods predominantly treat MICL as direct input-output mapping, overlooking the importance of explicitly inducing and reasoning over such rules, limiting both performance and interpretability. We propose ERIM, Explicit Rule-Induction for Multimodal In-Context Learning, a unified framework that enhances MICL by explicitly inducing the latent rules governing demonstration samples. Leveraging the reasoning ability of multi-modal large language model (MLLM), ERIM constructs rule-centric MICL datasets, introduces explicit supervision for rule induction, and fine-tunes MLLM to perform explicit rule-induction via a two-stage training strategy that combines mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments show consistent performance improvements across diverse MICL settings and demonstrate that correctly inducing underlying rules directly leads to stronger and more stable performance.

arXiv.title: CypherGuard: Database-Grounded Correction for Reliable Text-to-Cypher
arXiv.abstract: Text-to-Cypher translates natural-language questions into Cypher queries over property graphs. Graph database systems increasingly adopt this translation as a native query interface. Large language models generate fluent Cypher but stay unreliable. On Cypher-Bench a small model answers only 31.4% of questions correctly, and even a strong model plateaus at 71.76%. The dominant failure modes are structural rather than linguistic. For example, a generated query may parse correctly and follow the schema, yet still return zero rows because it traverses a relationship against the stored graph direction. To address this issue, we present CypherGuard, a training-free framework that detects and corrects these structural faults. Our approach uses two core components: a graph-native error taxonomy to guide repair, and a mined rule library to guide query generation. At inference time, CypherGuard first rewrites schema-detectable faults, then re-executes each draft and repairs it only when the query errors or returns nothing. On CypherBench test questions, across seven graphs, CypherGuard reaches 88.50% overall execution accuracy, +25.08% over the same-backbone zero-shot floor, surpassing an RL-fine-tuned 7B specialist and the strongest training-based system that we compare against.

arXiv.title: Scaly: an Optimizing Compiler for Optimal Control
arXiv.abstract: We present Scaly, an open-source optimizing compiler for optimal control, written in Python, that generates fast C code. Scaly provides a modeling language embedded in Python for the parametric optimization problems that arise in model predictive control and moving horizon estimation, and computes the sparse derivatives that standard optimization solvers need. Scaly accepts general nonlinear programs but applies optimizations specific to optimal control, which preserve the repeated structure of a problem, such as the stages of a horizon, through differentiation down to the generated loops. The generated C depends only on the C math library and never allocates memory dynamically. On three benchmark problems, Scaly evaluates the Hessian of the Lagrangian up to 26 times faster than CasADi, with smaller binaries and build times that stay nearly constant with the horizon. With the same solver, Scaly shortens the solver time per control step on every benchmark, by a factor of up to 9.

arXiv.title: Measuring What Matters: A Causal Reliance Score for Histopathology Image Segmentation
arXiv.comments: 15 pages, 8 figures, accepted into Medical Image Understanding and Analysis (MIUA) 2026 conference
arXiv.abstract: Reliable histopathology segmentation requires models that rely on pathology-relevant structures rather than spurious background correlations. In this work, we argue that improving architectures alone is insufficient if models continue to rely on spurious correlations rather than pathology-relevant features. We introduce a causality-inspired evaluation framework based on controlled interventions that explicitly probes model sensitivity to foreground tissue structure and background/domain variation. Building on this, we propose the Causal Reliance Score (CRS), a metric that quantifies the relative sensitivity of model predictions to foreground perturbation versus background/domain variation under controlled interventions. To support this analysis, we design augmentation strategies that act as implicit counterfactual interventions during training, encouraging invariance to nuisance factors while preserving morphology. We demonstrate how these interventions reveal behavioural differences between models that are not captured by standard metrics such as Dice or IoU. While we instantiate our framework using a self-supervised transformer (CAUSE-ViT), the primary contribution of this work is not a new architecture, but a principled intervention-based methodology and evaluation metric for auditing model behaviour in medical image segmentation. Our results suggest that evaluating model behaviour through counterfactual interventions is essential for developing reliable and clinically robust medical image segmentation systems.

arXiv.title: Visual-Inertial RGB-D SLAM with Encoders for a Differential Wheeled Robot
arXiv.comments: 11 pages. Author-accepted manuscript of the article published in IEEE Sensors Journal, 2022
arXiv.journal-ref: IEEE Sensors Journal, vol. 22, no. 6, pp. 5360-5371, March 2022
arXiv.abstract: Recent years have seen multiple impressive results in visual-inertial odometry (VIO) techniques, by which accurate state estimation can be achieved via the extended Kalman filter (EKF) or nonlinear optimization. However, these approaches are rarely open source, and they tend to fail in real experiments due to the temporary lack of feature points and fast motion. Therefore, in this study, we used encoders to overcome the temporary failure of purely vision-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). Here, we propose a generative measurement model for encoders and derive an expression for the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate and necessary Jacobians for optimization. We use our theory to present a novel tightly coupled visual-inertial encoder RGB-Depth (RGB-D) SLAM system. Tests on our system on an in-house dataset confirmed that our modeling effort led to accurate (with a root mean squared error (RMSE) of approximately 2-7 cm) and robust state estimation in real time. The source code and our dataset containing the encoder information have been published for verification.

arXiv.title: Stepwise-Querying: Distilling Reasoning without Access to Teacher Chain-of-Thought
arXiv.abstract: Reasoning distillation is widely used to transfer the reasoning capabilities of large language models to smaller students through teacher-generated supervision. In the black-box setting, however, teachers may expose only final answers and brief solutions, leaving intermediate calculations and validity conditions unavailable and thus limiting the reasoning supervision available for distillation. We propose Stepwise Querying, which elicits step-specific explanations without requiring access to the teacher's internal chain-of-thought (CoT) traces. Independent queries to the same teacher request intermediate derivations, validity checks, and corrections for individual steps, the assembled solutions are then used for standard supervised fine-tuning. Across two teachers, two students, and four mathematics and code benchmarks, our method achieves the highest score in 14 of 16 comparisons with three baselines. We further introduce Stepwise Explanation Information Gain (SEIG), a diagnostic based on the log-ratio of a frozen student's probabilities of correct step completion under stepwise and global explanations. Analyses on GSM8K show that incorrect-answer trajectories can remain useful when they preserve valid intermediate reasoning, while further decomposition yields limited additional gains.

arXiv.title: WorkIng: A Real-World and Synthetic Highway Work-Zone Benchmark Dataset for Autonomous Navigation
arXiv.comments: Accepted to WACV 2027. 19 pages including supplementary material. (c) 2027 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted
arXiv.abstract: Highway work zones are critical edge cases for autonomous vehicles (AVs), combining atypical geometries and jurisdiction-specific regulations that existing benchmarks fail to capture: real-world datasets lack 360° multi-modal, full-scene 3D work zone annotation, and no single recorded site can span the layouts and regulatory variants needed for generalizable models. We present WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark and training resource. WorkIng-Highway provides a 360° multi-modal work zone benchmark with synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras, and RTK-GPS across 32 km, yielding 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA complements this with procedural simulation spanning 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated by 100+ custom 3D assets. Benchmarking representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures shows that real-world data remains the primary performance driver, and that scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning. Resources: https://github.com/cvims/WorkIng

arXiv.title: MERIDIAN: Memory-Encoded Rituals for Intimacy across Distance in an Interactive, Asynchronous Neighbourhood
arXiv.comments: 13 pages, 14 figures, 5 tables. Playable game: https://jingyifan.love; source code: https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town
arXiv.abstract: How can shared memories become playable structures for partners who live in different time zones? We present MERIDIAN, a pre-deployment design case of Yi Town, a bilingual browser game developed by one member of a long-distance couple as a gift for the other. Nine levels translate personally meaningful events, places and cultural references into tasks within a navigable pixel town. A birthday prologue and a fictional wedding frame the intended experience. Drawing on research through design, we reconstruct four design changes from 109 development commits, 28 changelog versions and three design specifications. These records support six situated design commitments, including memory-derived mechanics, staged access, local progress storage and bilingual coverage. The implementation combines a union-based progress model with manually exchanged, checksummed codes and time-zone-dependent scenery. An implementation audit reproduced 153 passing unit tests and examined all 1,024 canonical progress codes, while identifying limits involving resets, unversioned level registries and residual transcription errors. The application has no author-operated backend for progress, but external media services and browser speech recognition limit its privacy and offline guarantees. No recipient evaluation or relationship outcomes are reported. The contribution is an inspectable account of design decisions and their trade-offs, including the tension between authoring a personal gift and preserving the recipient's freedom to interpret, decline or reshape it. The game is playable at https://jingyifan.love and its source is public at https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town.

arXiv.title: Characterizations and MacWilliams-Like Identities of Weakly Regular Bent Partitions
arXiv.abstract: Bent partitions play a significant role in the theory of bent functions. In this paper, we study weakly regular bent partitions, that is, all generated bent functions are weakly regular (called in class $\mathcal{WRBP}$). Let $Γ=\{A_{i}, i \in V_{m}\}$ be a bent partition of $V_{n}$ in class $\mathcal{WRBP}$, where $V_{n}$ denotes an $n$-dimensional vector space over the prime field $\mathbb{F}_{p}$, $n$ is even, $m \leq \frac{n}{2}$, and $m \geq 2$ if $p=2$. We first characterize bent partition $Γ$ in terms of the duals of component functions of vectorial bent functions. In particular, we prove that if $p \neq 3$, then all bent functions generated by $Γ$ are regular. Building on the above result, we give characterizations of bent partition $Γ$ in terms of two classes of linear codes. When $n \geq 4$ and $m=\frac{n}{2}$, except for the case where $(p, n)=(2, 4)$ and $|A_{i_{0}}|=1$ for some $i_{0}$, we show that $Γ$ is obtained from a spread (after a shift). Particularly, any normal bent partition of $V_{n}$ of depth $p^{\frac{n}{2}}$ in class $\mathcal{WRBP}$ must be obtained from a spread (after a shift), where $n \geq 4$. We establish the Macwilliams-like identities for bent partitions in class $\mathcal{WRBP}$. Furthermore, if $p$ is odd, we present some nonexistence results on bent partitions in class $\mathcal{WRBP}$.

arXiv.title: Clinical-Protocol-Aware Cyber Resilience for Connected Clinical Technologies Under AI-Enabled Adversarial Conditions
arXiv.categories: cs.AI cs.CE cs.ET cs.NI cs.SY eess.SY
arXiv.comments: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
arXiv.abstract: Healthcare increasingly relies on connected medical devices, clinical information systems, cloud services, and distributed-care technologies, creating cybersecurity risks across clinical workflows. AI-enabled capabilities can accelerate vulnerability discovery and attack-path analysis, increasing the need to limit compromise propagation. This paper proposes a clinical-protocol-aware cyber-resilience framework based on bounded clinical micro-networks and controlled interconnections. The framework integrates clinical factors into cybersecurity design, management, and evaluation, covering prevention, containment, and incident response. A parameterized Monte Carlo simulation distinguishes technical cyber exposure from modeled clinical consequence. Experiments investigate architectural connectivity, adversarial capability, security controls, protocol dependency, risk alignment, communication directionality, lifecycle integration, and response timing. Under the simulation assumptions, connected architecture increases mean cyber exposure by 56.3% relative to segmented architecture, while combined prevention and containment reduce exposure by 60.1% relative to no controls. Increasing protocol dependency raises the modeled clinical-impact index from 1.021 to 7.567 without changing mean cyber exposure, demonstrating that technical exposure and clinical consequence can diverge. Risk-alignment experiments further indicate higher modeled clinical impact when greater technical risk corresponds to greater clinical significance. The findings support comparative architectural analysis, not calibrated estimates of real-world cyber risk, control effectiveness, or patient harm. The framework provides a clinical-context-aware approach to security-boundary design, control prioritization, and coordinated containment in connected healthcare environments.

arXiv.title: Peeling the Matryoshka: Extracting Ontological Structure from Retrieval Embeddings
arXiv.comments: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 13 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Code: https://github.com/Eunchan24/PEEL
arXiv.abstract: Taxonomy construction is essential for knowledge-intensive NLP yet remains costly: clustering-based methods (i) need careful per-corpus tuning and yield unstable hierarchies, while LLM-based pipelines (ii) depend on expensive task-specific training that does not transfer across domains. We report an empirical finding that bears on both: in Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings, where each leading prefix is itself a usable, coarser vector, prefix length aligns with the coarse-to-fine granularity of gold taxonomies; shuffled- and reverse-dimension controls isolate the alignment to the learned early prefix dimensions. The pattern holds across three architecturally distinct MRL models. To test whether this regularity is usable, we introduce PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies): a minimal probe over these frozen embeddings, trained once with an order-embedding objective that represents hierarchy as vector containment; a minimum spanning arborescence then decodes taxonomic DAGs. Using only a concept vocabulary (no documents), PEEL recovers taxonomic DAGs with high structural fidelity on two OLLM benchmarks, transferring to a new domain with no target-edge supervision. The end-to-end OLLM pipeline, which jointly discovers concepts and induces structure from document corpora, is reported as a cross-task reference. Pre-trained retrieval embeddings encode a decodable granularity gradient; a minimal probe renders it as explicit parent-child (is-a) structure.

arXiv.title: Hard Sample-Conditioned Decorrelated Attention for Robust Face Recognition
arXiv.comments: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027)
arXiv.abstract: Multi-head attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) allows independent attention patterns across heads, but without explicit regularization, heads may learn redundant patterns rather than complementary roles. Correlation-based penalties encourage head disentanglement, yet apply uniform regularization across all training samples. In face recognition (FR), hard samples whose embeddings lie close to competing identities are critical for optimization and generalization. Motivated by this, we propose ViT-HarDis, which conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty: samples with high cosine similarity to negative class centers receive stronger head decorrelation, enforcing specialization where identity ambiguity is highest. Experiments show improvements over both the baseline and uniform disentanglement on most benchmarks. Our analysis shows that ViT-HarDis reduces the similarity of hard samples to competing class centers while decreasing inter-head attention similarity, and that applying disentanglement only to the final transformer layers outperforms regularizing the entire network. Trained on WebFace4M, ViT-HarDis achieves SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank-1, while achieving the best IJB-B and TinyFace results when trained on MS1MV3, improving FR without architectural modifications or additional inference cost. Code: https://github.com/TaharChettaoui/Hard-Sample-Conditioned-Attention-for-FR.

arXiv.title: Different Models, Shared Failures: Auditing Frozen-Encoder Pools for Medical Segmentation
arXiv.comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 47 pages, 8 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/eunseobchoi/CoFailMed
arXiv.abstract: Average segmentation accuracy and model count do not reveal whether models fail on the same cases. We present CoFailMed, an audit of correlated failures in pretrained-encoder pools for medical segmentation. Across five 2D tasks, we evaluate 11 public pretrained encoders (a controlled sample, not a census) using frozen features and separately trained $1\times 1$ readouts with four seeds per encoder. Shared-checkpoint pairs have the highest mean per-case Dice correlation. An expanded 17-encoder analysis shows that distinct checkpoints within the same encoder family remain more correlated than cross-family pairs. At the pooled 33rd-percentile Dice threshold, four-member pools drawn from distinct encoders have mean effective sizes of 1.56-2.92, estimated from failure correlations in pools with enough failures and passes per member. In the primary pool, richer readouts and fine-tuning narrow the Dice-correlation gap between pairs sharing a checkpoint (or the DINOv2-B/S release) and all other pairs. Yet dependence between different encoders can increase, and fine-tuning does not consistently increase effective pool size at 33rd-percentile thresholds recomputed for each training recipe. A smaller between-group gap can coexist with greater dependence. Pool evaluation should therefore report absolute dependence and threshold-specific effective size alongside accuracy and nominal pool size. The CoFailMed release provides aligned per-case traces, analysis scripts and study code to reproduce the central audit results.

arXiv.title: Implicit Assumptions About Tasks in Continual Learning
arXiv.comments: Accepted to the Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents at NeurIPS 2026
arXiv.abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.

arXiv.title: Whose Values, Which Contexts, and What Signals? Grounding Cultural Value Alignment with Re3Culture
arXiv.abstract: Cultural value alignment requires not only model optimization but also a well-specified target grounded in real-human evidence. Yet how such targets should be grounded in human data remains largely unexplored, raising three fundamental questions: (1) whose values should be represented? (2) where should cultural values be observed? and (3) what signals reveal underlying values? We investigate these questions through Re3Culture, a large-scale dataset linking (i) Representative communities: 700+ human participants across four cultures recruited through cultural-affiliation screening and demographic-aware sampling; (ii) Realistic scenario: culturally sensitive scenarios selected by community members, e.g., family and kinship; and (iii) Revealed value signals: 1,400+ value surveys, 20,000+ topic-grounded behavioral principles and explicit value priorities with responses for 6,000+ situated questions. Our analysis shows why these choices matter for defining the target, with three implications. First, estimating cultural values requires both community affiliation and broad internal coverage. Substituting other cultures or restricting subgroup coverage shifts value estimates. LLM simulations also disproportionately reflect particular subgroups. Second, values must be observed in concrete, community-guided situations. Abstract questionnaire profiles weakly recover situated priorities, and communities differ in which scenarios they identify as culturally value-revealing. Third, value priorities should be elicited explicitly, not learned from response preferences or bottom-line answers alone. Preferences conflate value agreement with other response-level qualities, and similar answers can be derived from different value priorities. By addressing these requirements, Re3Culture provides the first human-grounded resource that explicitly informs target definition for cultural value alignment.

arXiv.title: Accurate and Auditable ECG Classification via Visibility Graph Neural Networks
arXiv.comments: 43 pages, 10 figures, 21 tables, including Supplementary Information
arXiv.abstract: Physicians read electrocardiograms (ECGs) from waveform shape and timing, yet accurate deep-learning classifiers rarely show which waveform regions drive their predictions. We introduce LYNX-ECG, a graph neural network that represents each heartbeat as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points. On CODE-Test, LYNX-ECG reaches a macro F1 score of 0.889, outperforming five baselines including the ECGFounder foundation model, while its graphs need about 14% of the storage of graphs built from every sample. Because each node maps to a specific ECG time, we can delete clinically defined waveform regions and alter beat timing to audit predictions. For conduction disorders, the clinically expected region was the strongest evidence in more than 90% of correct predictions. Bradycardia and tachycardia calls follow heart rate with conduction intervals held fixed, and atrial fibrillation calls vanish when beat-to-beat variation is removed. Sparse visibility graphs thus pair accurate ECG classification with clinically grounded, testable explanations.

arXiv.title: A two-stage diffusion-driven morphogenesis model with evolving connectivity
arXiv.comments: Submitted to Applied Mathematical Modelling. Animation available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23808711
arXiv.abstract: Morphogenesis of diatom silica shells involves a sequence of topological transitions: initially separate ribs grow and branch, then merge through bridges, leaving a regular network of pores. Existing models based on diffusion-limited aggregation or reaction-diffusion reproduce either branching or pore formation, but not both within a single framework. Here we propose a two-stage model of diffusion-driven morphogenesis with evolving connectivity. The model is formulated on a fixed finite element mesh with a density field on an active layer. Stage 1 reproduces dendritic growth, where a stimulus based on the local diffusive flux exceeds a threshold. Stage 2 uses an inverted stimulus, where high local flux suppresses precipitation, stabilizing pores between the dendrites. The update rules are analogous to sensitivity in density-based topology optimization and to strain energy density in bone remodeling. The model predicts distinct morphological regimes on each stage, controlled by the respective thresholds. For a reference calculation, the predicted pore network is regular, with approximately uniform spacing, and pores are absent near the domain edges, consistent with observations on diatom valves. The model provides a unified framework for describing both stages of silica morphogenesis and suggests a route for comparing computational predictions with cryo-electron tomography data.

arXiv.title: On-device Detection of Wearer-induced NLOS on Chest-worn UWB Tags: Machine Learning, Link Indicators, or Both?
arXiv.comments: Submitted to ACM Transactions on Sensor Networks
arXiv.abstract: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.

arXiv.title: Reparo: Synthesizing and Validating Access Control Policies
arXiv.abstract: Writing correct access control policies for software applications is difficult because it requires expertise in the authorization language and a thorough understanding of the application's authorization requirements. Existing synthesis and mining approaches assume explicit authorization inputs and a trusted reference policy. However, authorization logic is often distributed across code, comments, and documentation rather than captured in a single artifact, and developer-defined policies in real-world application repositories are often incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. We present Reparo, an LLM-aided pipeline for access control policy synthesis, repair, and validation. Reparo collects repository evidence for authorization intent and uses it to guide an LLM in generating an initial policy. It then uses official policy-language validation tools to identify and automatically repair errors. For semantic validation, a different LLM derives a behavioral oracle from the same repository evidence, consisting of concrete authorization requests with expected allow or deny decisions, which Reparo executes against the generated policy. We manually assess the oracle on a statistically sized sample of 390 test cases. We evaluate Reparo on 228 real-world GitHub repositories that use Cedar, OpenFGA, or Rego. In these repositories, 40.6-55.7% of the repository policies fail their language's validation tool, whereas Reparo produces 99.0-100% valid policies after repair. Agreement with the oracle is 98.2-99.6% for OpenFGA, 82.0-86.5% for Cedar, and 76.3-80.2% for Rego. Manual review confirms 91.5-96.9% of the sampled test cases as correct. Synthesizing and validating the policy for one repository takes about five minutes and costs $0.55-$1.57. These results show that repository evidence can support both access policy synthesis and independent validation, even when no reliable reference policy exists.

arXiv.title: Towards Out-of-Distribution Uncertainty Quantification for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials via Pre-Training
arXiv.abstract: Informative uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for the practical deployment of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), as it provides insight into their reliability across chemical space. Although numerous post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods for MLIPs have recently been proposed, most have been trained in low-data regimes, restricting their applicability to narrow domains of interest. Inspired by the emergence of foundational MLIPs, we propose pre-training uncertainty estimators on large, diverse datasets to enable broader applicability. We pre-train several UQ models on large materials science datasets to quantify the uncertainty of different MLIPs, and evaluate their performance on both in-distribution and out-of-domain (OOD) adsorption-energy predictions. We find that pre-trained uncertainty estimators provide viable zero-shot uncertainty estimates across multiple datasets, while fine-tuning consistently yields positive correlations between predicted uncertainty and prediction error, even on the most challenging datasets. These results lay the groundwork for foundational UQ models for MLIPs, ultimately facilitating their deployment in practical settings by providing users with a priori information about model reliability and applicability.

arXiv.title: What Standard Evaluations Hide About Detectors of Hijacked LLM Agents: Rare Attacks, Unseen Tools and Benchmark Transfer
arXiv.comments: 14 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code, data and every monitor call: https://github.com/Mahmoud-Abbasi-svg/agent-trace-detector-eval
arXiv.abstract: Detectors can flag hijacked large language model (LLM) agents from the traces of the tools they call. In the eleven evaluations we audited, attacks or anomalies make up 16% to 86% of the test samples, no evaluation varies that share, and six report no test on data from a second benchmark or source. We ask what such evaluations hide. On the AgentDrift and AgentDojo benchmarks we test trained detectors that read tool identities, behavior, call sequences, step embeddings or text, and a released LLM action monitor, AlignmentCheck, with thresholds fixed on training data or set by the monitor's released decision rule. First, at a 2% attack rate a detector with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.879 reaches a precision of 0.076, and the mix of negatives alone moves that precision between 0.039 and 0.117. Second, as tool coverage, the share of test tool calls whose tool was seen in training, falls, detector rankings cross near 50% coverage and reverse below it, because unseen tools map to inputs that training never reached. Dropout on tool inputs largely removes the reversal. Third, no detector trained on AgentDrift ranks AgentDojo traces better than chance (AUROC 0.47 to 0.52), including one that reaches 0.996 within AgentDojo. The monitor, trained on neither, reaches 0.930, but with its open backbone its released decision rule would still mostly raise false alerts at a 2% attack rate (precision 0.096). We turn these findings into a checklist for evaluating trace detectors.

arXiv.title: Backpropagation-free Deep Learning for Time-Series Classification
arXiv.abstract: Deep neural networks for time series classification (TSC) are trained almost exclusively by error backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem. Backpropagation-free learning rules such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired NoProp relax these constraints but have been evaluated almost exclusively on 2D image benchmarks. We adapt these three learners to univariate TSC with 1D convolutional architectures and present the first systematic study of them across 112 datasets from the UCR time series archive, with one hyperparameter-optimized configuration per method. The optimized learners reach mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84). We propose an analysis framework that relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime to dataset properties and tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, measured as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture. Intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap for all three learners (partial Spearman $ρ$ from $0.28$ to $0.40$). Pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD $-0.025$ and $-0.055$), consistent with near-random convolutional features, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does (DD $+0.013$). Relative to backpropagation on the same architectures, DRTP reduces training floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA yields no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.

arXiv.title: Exploring Bad Minima in Transfer Learning
arXiv.comments: 57 pages, 13 figures, 3 tables. MPhil thesis, University of Cambridge, 2022. Supervised by Ferenc Huszár
arXiv.abstract: Transfer learning is a highly successful learning paradigm in deep learning which leverages knowledge from one task and applies it to another. Despite its success, the necessary conditions for knowledge transfer are unclear and require further research. In this dissertation, our aim is to understand transferability a little better by answering the following question: Does good generalization on a source task necessarily imply transferability to a related target task? We hypothesize the answer is negative, and attempt to find counterexamples via adversarial attacks on the transfer learning procedure. Over three types of adversarial attacks, our empirical results show a strong relationship between generalization on the source task and transferability. These results do not rule out generalization on the source task as a sufficient condition for successful transfer.

arXiv.title: Continual Reinforcement Learning Is an Integration Problem
arXiv.comments: 39 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Playable companion and source code: https://github.com/fractalbrain-ai/10d-game
arXiv.abstract: This paper presents an opinionated set of ten desiderata intended to inform the design and evaluation of reinforcement-learning agents that learn continually throughout a continuing lifetime. We use these desiderata to examine a representative selection of existing approaches. Progress on individual desiderata is valuable, but the longer-term aim should be to integrate all ten within a single agent. To our knowledge, no published evaluation has yet provided evidence for such an integration. Likewise, the representative benchmarks we review probe different parts of this target, but separate evaluations do not establish that the corresponding properties coexist within one agent throughout a continuing lifetime. As a secondary contribution, we therefore present a compact persistent-world scenario as a playable companion to the desiderata and outline a proposed benchmark that examines a broad range of associated behavioral capabilities together within one such lifetime.

arXiv.title: Degree Realization with Maximum Matching
arXiv.abstract: The Maximum Matching Degree Realization problem requires, for a sequence $d$ of $n$ positive integers, to compute a realizing graph(whose degree sequence corresponds to $d$) with the maximum possible matching. We present a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. The decision version of this problem requires to determine whether a sequence $d$ admits a realization with a matching of size $ν$ (without computing such a realization). Recently, it was shown that it can be done by verifying a series of inequalities. We improve the existing characterization by reducing the number of inequalities.

arXiv.title: RECAST: REconstruction of Chain-of-Thought via Auditable Structured Traces
arXiv.abstract: Large closed-source reasoning models expose only their final answers. The intermediate reasoning that produces those answers is hidden behind API surfaces, tool-call policies, and safety filters. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) extraction methods assume a side channel: a visible reasoning field, a scratchpad carried through tool calls, or a signed/encrypted reasoning block. We reproduce three representative state-of-the-art extraction methods and find that, on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 accessed through the standard chat-completions interface, all three return zero CoT tokens. The failure is structural rather than a bug: the reasoning field is absent, named tool selection is rejected, free-text scratchpad arguments are filtered, and no replayable reasoning block is exposed. We therefore take a different route. We present RECAST, a reconstruction-based framework that conditions a decoder on the question and the target model's final answer, reconstructs a first-person structured rationale, cleans it, and builds SFT-ready data. To the best of our knowledge, RECAST is the first system to reconstruct CoT from frontier closed models such as Claude-Sonnet-5.5, GPT-6.1, and Gemini 3 without using hidden reasoning channels. We instantiate RECAST on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 and additionally obtain successful qualitative reconstructions on GPT-6.1 and Gemini 3 with the same answer-only protocol. The system is open-source and packaged as an agent skill: one prompt deploys it and runs the complete pipeline to produce SFT-ready CoT data. This preprint describes the system, its threat model, and a controlled artifact validation; it does not claim large-scale benchmark improvements.

arXiv.title: A Patch is More Than a Token
arXiv.comments: 54 pages, 16 figures, 12 tables. Code and experimental assets: https://github.com/zixiongwang-ai/PMTT
arXiv.abstract: Vision Transformers represent each image patch through a canonical token produced under one observation condition. That token is a powerful interface, but it is still one realized state of the patch. We introduce PMTT, which establishes two foundations: a patch representation object can extend from one canonical state to a canonical-centered Representation State Family, and identity-preserving variation opens Patch-Level Local Feature Space. We develop four parts of this representation program. Patch Information Acquisition and Dense Orbital Views expose lawful same-patch states. Visible-to-Hidden prediction tests whether observed states reveal structure beyond themselves. Intrinsic analysis identifies low-dimensional, energy-concentrated, patch-specific, predictive geometry. Representation Organization separates acquiring more information from organizing that information, with an analytic Manifold as the central structured representation. We realize PMTT on frozen DINOv3 S/B/L/H+ backbones without neural post-training of the representation. Across two independent 4,096-anchor cohorts, Manifold explains 70.8-79.6% of Hidden variation, compared with 55.0-72.3% for directly Observed states, and wins on more than 95% of anchors at every scale. Effective rank falls from about 2.5 to 2.0 while dominant energy concentration rises with backbone scale. Across six visual capabilities and four scales, Observed exceeds the canonical Center in 21 of 24 conditions, Manifold exceeds Center in 23, and Manifold exceeds Observed in 16. The strongest current consequence appears in physical correspondence, where MegaDepth satisfies Center < Observed < Manifold at every scale. These results show that pretrained visual backbones contain richer patch information than the standard single-token interface directly exposes. Code and experimental assets are available at https://github.com/zixiongwang-ai/PMTT.

arXiv.title: DIFFNAS: Predictor-Free Neural Architecture Search via Diffusion Model and Zero-Cost Evaluation
arXiv.comments: 13 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Yize Sun and Hanzhang Ma contributed equally
arXiv.abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has advanced the automated design of deep networks, but remains computationally expensive due to reliance on model training or performance predictors. We introduce DIFFNAS, a predictor-free NAS framework that leverages a discrete graph diffusion model guided by zero-cost performance proxies. Unlike prior diffusion-based NAS methods that require learned performance predictors, DIFFNAS conditions the generative process on training-free metrics such as MeCo and SWAP, enabling efficient architecture search with minimal computational overhead. Experiments on NAS-Bench-201 show that DIFFNAS finds the optimal architectures for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (94.37% and 73.51%) without a pretrained predictor, while reducing search cost by up to 17.5x compared to DiffusionNAG. On the MobileNetV3 search space, its accuracy is lower than that of DiffusionNAG. These results highlight the promise of diffusion models combined with zero-cost proxies for scalable and effective architecture search.

arXiv.title: ElTab: Elastically Looped Tabular Transformers
arXiv.abstract: Tabular transformer models such as TabPFN achieve strong predictive performance but incur substantial inference costs, making them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained settings. While looped transformers reduce parameter count through weight sharing, they can lose significant predictive power when stopped early. To address this challenge, we introduce the Elastically Looped Tabular Transformer (ElTab), a single model trained to operate across different computational budgets through supervision at randomly sampled early exits. Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, a single ElTab model matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half, and matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs. These results show that elastic-depth training yields a single model that adapts to the deployment budget at hand, offering a favorable trade-off among predictive performance, storage, and computational cost.

arXiv.title: Compressing the Lawler-Moore Dynamic Program for Weighted Tardy Jobs
arXiv.abstract: The classic scheduling problem of minimizing the total weight of tardy jobs ($P_m||\sum_jw_jU_j$) asks for a schedule of jobs each with a processing time, weight, and due date on a constant number of parallel identical machines. A job is late in a schedule if it completes after its due date, and an optimal schedule is one where the total weight of all late jobs is minimized. The classic dynamic programming algorithm of Lawler and Moore [Manag. Sci., 1969] solves this problem in $O(nd_{\max}^m)$ where $n$ is the number of jobs, $d_{\max}$ is the maximum due date of any job, and $m$ is the number of identical machines. We show that it is sufficient to only compute part of the dynamic program and obtain the running time $\tilde{O}(n + d_{\max}^{m + 1})$ where $\tilde{O}$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This affirmatively answers the open question posed by Hermelin, Molter, and Shabtay [INFORMS J. Comput., 2024], whether a running time of $\tilde{O}(n + d_{\max}^2)$ is possible on a single machine.

arXiv.title: Trainable Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
arXiv.journal-ref: Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases. Research Track. ECML PKDD 2026. Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 16944, pp 245-259. Springer, Cham
arXiv.abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes.
