At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.

arXiv.title: Any Forcing: Any-Step Generality and One-Step Stability for Autoregressive Video Generation
arXiv.abstract: Autoregressive video generation enables efficient inference through streaming prediction. However, existing methods are typically restricted to fixed sampling steps, limiting the flexibility to balance generation quality and efficiency, while one-step generation suffers from degraded visual quality and error accumulation over long sequences, leading to content drift and generation collapse. To address these issues, we propose Any Forcing, a unified framework for achieving Any-Step Generality and One-Step Stability. Specifically, we introduce a unified adversarial discriminator that jointly performs real-distribution alignment, inter-step consistency alignment, and first-frame quality enhancement, enabling flexible sampling while preserving one-step generation quality. Furthermore, we propose a training-free adaptive long-term memory selection mechanism that selects historical states based on global semantic relevance and local value contribution, while remapping their temporal positions to preserve temporal relationships within the memory cache, thereby enabling stable one-step long-video generation. Experiments demonstrate that Any Forcing achieves high-quality and stable one-step autoregressive video generation, achieving 20.9 FPS and 24.7 FPS for short and long video generation on a single H100 GPU, respectively.

arXiv.title: Beyond Smart Homes: Characterizing IoT Vulnerabilities Across Sectors, Vendors, and Products
arXiv.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has expanded beyond consumer smart homes to sectors, such as industrial systems, healthcare, and smart cities, broadening the IoT attack surface. Prior empirical work has focused on studying aggregate IoT vulnerability characteristics or specific protocols, so patching is directed by aggregate security guidance. However, if dominant weaknesses differ substantially across sectors or products, such uniform guidance misdirects the remediation effort. To address this gap, we present a fine-grained, data-driven analysis of IoT vulnerabilities using a dataset of more than 15,000 IoT specific CVEs. We design a pipeline to enrich noisy CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) metadata, normalizing vendors and products, then assigning product type and sector labels using lexical matching, fuzzy clustering, and LLM-assisted classification. We find meaningful differences in the weakness profile of IoT sectors. For example, healthcare is dominated by authentication and credential weaknesses, while automotive faces memory issues. More importantly, we find that weakness profiles are more similar across different product types from the same vendor than across the same product type built by different vendors. This suggests vendor-level factors such as shared code and development practices dominate weakness inheritance, making a vendor's disclosure history informative about its other products. Our findings suggest weakness classes should be used to prioritize remediation efforts.

arXiv.title: Treedepth is NP-Hard on Planar Graphs of Maximum Degree 3
arXiv.abstract: Treedepth is an important parameter in algorithmic graph theory. It is known that the problem of computing the treedepth of a graph is NP-hard. It has been an open problem whether treedepth can be computed in polynomial time when the input graph is restricted to be planar, or of bounded degree. Assuming $P \neq NP$, we answer both questions in the negative: Under polynomial-time Turing reductions, it is NP-hard to compute the treedepth of planar graphs with maximum degree 3. This degree bound is best possible, since treedepth can be computed efficiently on graphs of maximum degree 2.

arXiv.title: Learning Clean Generative Processes from Noisy Measurements
arXiv.abstract: We study how to learn a generative model of clean images using only noisy observations. Diffusion processes and their generalizations to non-Gaussian noise require posterior predictions at every noise level. We first show that it is possible to learn these predictions from independent noisy views using Noise2Noise regression, but only at or above the noise level of the training data. To learn the predictions below that level, needed to generate clean images, we impose consistency: a prediction should equal its expectation after continuing the sampling process. We derive conditions under which consistency uniquely determines the continuation to the clean image distribution and verify them for Poisson, binomial, Gamma, and negative-binomial measurements. Experiments on CIFAR-10, photon-counting microscopy, and synthetic aperture radar show that the required posterior predictions can be learned from noisy views alone and that the consistency relation repairs the continuation beyond the noise level of the data, which severely deteriorates without consistency.

arXiv.title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
arXiv.journal-ref: Proceedings of the Ninth AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026)
arXiv.abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code.

arXiv.title: Near-Optimal Second-Order Convex Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
arXiv.abstract: We study the stochastic second-order oracle complexity of solving smooth convex finite-sum optimization with $n$ components. Very recently, Tsedenov \& Kovalev (2026) showed that the minimax optimal complexity under averaged smoothness and convexity is $\tildeΘ(n + n^{6/7} ε^{-2/7})$ by establishing nearly matching upper and lower bounds. In this paper, we show that individual smoothness and convexity provably enable further acceleration, where the lower complexity bound is $Ω(n+ n^{5/7} ε^{-2/7})$ under this stronger assumption. Then, by establishing a novel second-order self-bounding inequality, we design a new Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method, which can lead to a better complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + n^{5/7} ε^{-2/7})$ by applying the optimal Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration, matching our lower bound up to only logarithmic factors.

arXiv.title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo
arXiv.comments: 35 pages, 16 figures, 7 tables; supplementary tables and figures included
arXiv.abstract: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid proxies for biodiversity, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly. We revise and test an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI) built from species-level detections. Its primary form, ABI_E, is Shannon diversity of detections normalised by the regional species pool expected at the site and season (H / ln S_ref); temporal stability T is reported as a separate component. We first benchmarked four classifiers on a strongly labelled tropical dataset (1,216 calls, 24 classes) with recording-grouped cross-validation. BirdNET embeddings + logistic regression performed best (macro-F1 0.750 +/- 0.029), and random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70. We then applied BirdNET v2.4 with a location and season filter to recordings from a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe, and from three habitats at Emirates Park Zoo and Resort, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. A stricter post-hoc location filter removed 517 high-confidence detections of 9 implausible species, all at the zoo. After diel-matched rarefaction to equal effort (6 h), the savanna site held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3-13 species (ABI_E = 0.03-0.21) at the zoo sites. Across 149 recorded hours, ABI_E correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), whereas six standard indices did not (best: ACI, rho = 0.48). The stability term was lower at the savanna site (0.39) than at the zoo (0.65-0.67), showing that it penalises the natural diel cycle of bird activity. Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a declared regional reference pool and effort standardisation provide a more interpretable biodiversity indicator than energy-based acoustic indices.

arXiv.title: Proof-Carrying Evolution: Black-Box Search, White-Box Flight
arXiv.abstract: We study whether a language model can help design controllers whose behavior can be formally checked. In proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a search proposes controllers together with their certificates. Their mathematical forms are fixed; a proposer chooses their numerical parameters together. Certificate checks guide selection, and only a certified candidate can be returned. The deployed artifact is a control law and its certificate; the language model is used only during design. We compare four language models with classical search and synthesis on docking under a speed limit, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), using paired runs and shared proposal allowances. Certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic during search on the linear problems. On SO(3), the search uses floating-point checks, followed by exact re-verification of every reported champion. The best run of each method also receives Lean 4 proofs of its stated control properties. On the linear problems, the strongest models beat the standard classical baselines on every run, but a classical optimizer that chooses certificates for the same objective closes most of that lead. Among the cited pursuit champions, the ranking does not survive a change from Euler to zero-order-hold dynamics. On SO(3), no model detectably outperforms CMA-ES when mixed with classical mutation. When models write every proposal, one tested model improves on CMA-ES and the other performs worse than its mixed variant. All search medians remain below the hand-tuned law. In a docking control with the objective and mutation operator held fixed, retaining certified candidates yields new certified designs in every run; removing this rule yields none.

arXiv.title: Optimal Online Weighted Connectivity Augmentation
arXiv.abstract: In the online Weighted Connectivity Augmentation Problem (WCAP), we are given a $k$-edge-connected graph on $n$ vertices and a set of additional edges, called links, with nonnegative costs. Pairs of vertices arrive one by one, and an online algorithm must immediately and irrevocably buy links so that each pair becomes $(k+1)$-edge-connected. The goal is to minimize the total cost of the purchased links. We obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for WCAP, improving the previous $O(\log^2 n)$ bound (SODA 2026). Our bound is asymptotically optimal, even for randomized algorithms in the random-order model. The general problem reduces to the case where the underlying graph is a cycle, for which link costs in $\{0,1\}$ already yield an $Ω(\log n)$ lower bound. Surprisingly, for unit costs on a cycle, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $4$-competitive algorithm, improving the previous $O(\log n)$ bound (SODA 2026), and prove that this ratio is optimal among deterministic algorithms. Thus, with unit costs, cycles are easier than trees, where the optimal competitive ratio is $Θ(\log n)$.

arXiv.title: System-Level Factors Influencing AGC Cyber-Attack Success and RAS Vulnerability in Multi-Area Grids
arXiv.journal-ref: CIGRE 2026 Paris Session (Paper D2-10223)
arXiv.abstract: Automatic generation control (AGC) stabilizes frequency and scheduled power exchanges among interconnected areas, yet its reliance on communication networks introduces cyber-vulnerabilities. This work examines coordinated AGC cyber-attacks in the presence of remedial action schemes (RAS) and identifies operating conditions under which an attacker can drive grid frequency beyond safe limits while evading RAS. A feedback-based attack policy is used to manipulate AGC signals and steer system frequency toward unsafe trajectories. Then, a large nested-loop parametric sweep---spanning attacked-area inertia relative to its interconnected neighboring area, AGC capacity versus maximum tie-line transfer, AGC update rate, load damping, and bi-directional power transfers---generates over 1.45 million scenarios. These are classified using a decision tree to establish guidelines to distinguish successful from unsuccessful attacks based on frequency deviations. The resulting vulnerability guidelines are validated on a three-area system using phasor-domain simulations with IEEE 9-bus area models, detailed turbine--governor dynamics, and under/over-frequency load and generation shedding. Results show that specific combinations of AGC capacity, inertia distribution, and pre-attack tie-line loading increase the likelihood of successful attacks, offering operators actionable criteria for identifying vulnerable operating conditions.

arXiv.title: Exact Theory and Optimal Stepsizes for Stochastic Gradient Descent in Smooth Convex Minimization
arXiv.abstract: This work considers the design of stepsize schedules for stochastic gradient descent in smooth convex optimization. Throughout, we assume that gradient noise is conditionally zero-mean with bounded variance. Among problems with dimension $d\geq N+1$, we provide an exact worst-case analysis of the expected suboptimality of stochastic gradient descent's final iterate. Our analysis applies to any (potentially nonconstant) schedule of $N$ stepsizes in $[0,1.5]^N$. Here, exact means that we provide a matching objective function and noise distributions where our guarantee is attained. Whenever the variance bound is at least $Ω(1/\sqrt{N})$, our theory provides the minimax optimal stepsize schedule for stochastic gradient descent and proves its uniqueness. These optimal stepsizes monotonically decrease, ruling out any accelerations in expected final suboptimality from fixed fractal schedules observed in the deterministic case.

arXiv.title: A Hybrid Path Planning Framework for Assistive Wheelchair Navigation in Dynamic Pedestrian Environments
arXiv.comments: 14 pages, 5 figures. Presented as a main-track paper at the International Conference of Social Robotics + ART'26, London, UK, 1-4 July 2026
arXiv.abstract: Autonomous wheelchairs can improve the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments by providing greater independence. However, reliable navigation especially in human environments is a major challenge due to factors such as dynamic obstacles, unpredictable pedestrian behavior, and the users' need to complete multiple stops along the way before reaching their final destination. This paper presents a hybrid path planning framework for multi-goal navigation in dynamic environments. The framework integrates the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for global task ordering with the Potential Field (PF) method and heuristic local planners such as Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) to achieve collision-free navigation. Within this hybrid framework, TSP determines the visiting order of intermediate stations, PF transfers global path information, and local planners avoid obstacles while guiding the robot to the stations. The local planners generate feasible paths that allow the robot to follow the global trajectory and reroute to avoid static and dynamic obstacles. For this purpose, two algorithms have been developed: (i) TSP-PF-RRT and (ii) TSP-PF-A*. The performance of the proposed algorithms are evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded scenarios that contain heterogeneous dynamic and static obstacles. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid framework enables efficient multi-goal navigation while maintaining safe operation in dynamic environments with humans, with TSP-PF-RRT achieving fewer or no collisions and shorter travel distances.

arXiv.title: REA: A Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control
arXiv.abstract: Foundation models are becoming remarkably reliable at high-level reasoning, yet they remain too slow and costly to serve as fine-grained controllers. Conversely, fast policies like VLAs and whole-body controllers offer more efficient reflexes, but struggle to generalize. While pairing a deliberative brain (foundation models) with a reactive cerebellum (fast policies) seems natural for embodied systems, two obstacles remain: methods are built and scored on incompatible stacks, and their asynchronous coordination is difficult. For example, an agent that calls the VLA in the agentic loop can stall the fast execution, while a VLA that calls the agent on errors tends to re-trigger fallbacks repeatedly or completely miss silent failures. To address this, we propose REA (Routed Embodied Agent), a unified runtime where a deliberative System 2, an embodied router System 1 and reactive System 0 policies cooperate under a single golden rule - no running policy waits on the brain. Instead of querying the brain at each failure, REA employs a route memory that stores each policy's measured success ahead of time, a boundary-triggered judge gate that consults the brain on policy execution, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery. Evaluated on 3,000 test episodes across 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success and beats the best single-agent baseline in its own policy pool (94.7%) while reducing control steps by 25% and control time by 17%. In a separate 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study, REA achieves 84% success with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, compared with 80% for the strongest single VLA baseline MEDex. These results demonstrate learned and programmatic policies operating within the same runtime. REA also transfers to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving the highest observed success among the compared methods.

arXiv.title: CRoS: Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs Improves Accuracy and Reasoning Faithfulness
arXiv.comments: 17 pages, 3 figures, 14 tables. Project page: https://xxiaoyuuuu.github.io/CRoS-Page
arXiv.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the standard method for training language models to reason. However, RLVR typically relies solely on outcome correctness, which does not guarantee that the CoT causally contributes to the final answer. Without this connection, outcome rewards may fail to reinforce high-quality reasoning. Existing causality metrics assess CoT causality by perturbing the CoT, such as deleting reasoning steps or injecting errors, and measuring changes in the final answer. However, these perturbations inevitably alter information in each step. Consequently, high causality scores may reflect sensitivity to information changes introduced by perturbation rather than true causality. Such confounding effects further induce undesirable reasoning behaviors when these metrics are used as training rewards, including generating less informative CoTs and reducing exploration and self-correction. To address this problem, we propose CRoS (Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs), a novel CoT causality metric that perturbs the order of reasoning steps without altering content, thereby preserving information within each step. On Reasoning Gym with Gemma-3-4B, CRoS outperforms existing causality and outcome rewards in out-of-domain accuracy, CoT quality, and CoT faithfulness. Specifically, CRoS achieves 46.8% accuracy on five unseen logic and games datasets, outperforming the strongest baseline (43.8%). It also achieves better CoT quality, consistently outperforming baselines in CoT-Pass@K from K=1 to 128, averaging 43.4% vs. 41.4%. For CoT faithfulness, CRoS achieves a hint acknowledgment score of 34.0% vs. 20.2%.

arXiv.title: Rapid mixing of Potts Glauber dynamics throughout uniqueness
arXiv.abstract: Sampling from the ferromagnetic $q$-state Potts model is a fundamental problem in statistical physics and approximate counting. Although computationally hard in the worst case, sampling is expected to be efficient throughout the high-temperature uniqueness regime of the model using the natural single-site Glauber dynamics. We establish fast mixing bounds for every $q$, in the full high-temperature regimes in the two central graph families on $n$ vertices. (1) For every $Δ\ge 3$, the Potts Glauber dynamics mixes in $n\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ steps with high probability on a uniformly random $Δ$-regular graph for all $β<β_u(q,\mathbb T_Δ)$ where $β_u(q,\mathbb T_Δ)$ is the uniqueness threshold on the $Δ$-regular tree; (2) For every $d\ge 2$, the Potts Glauber dynamics has inverse spectral gap $n^{1+o(1)}$ on cubes or tori in $\mathbb Z^d$ for all $β<β_c(q,\mathbb Z^d)$ where $β_c(q,\mathbb Z^d)$ is the critical point on $\mathbb Z^d$. Both temperature thresholds are sharp as the Glauber dynamics slows down exponentially above them. These results overcome the challenge of bounding mixing times without access to correlation decay bounds in the presence of pinnings (i.e., without spectral independence or strong spatial mixing). For this purpose, our proof introduces a new dichotomy principle: throughout the high-temperature regime, any initial spin distribution is either such that its pinnings ensure good correlation decay, or Glauber dynamics escapes from that distribution quickly. We expect this kind of dichotomy to have further applications. As a demonstration, we also develop its analog for random-cluster dynamics and use it to prove that Swendsen-Wang dynamics on random $Δ$-regular graphs mixes in $O(\log n)$ time throughout uniqueness. The results in this paper were arrived at with the assistance of ChatGPT 5.6 and 6.

arXiv.title: PersonaChatBench: Evaluating Chat Assistants with Diverse Simulated Users
arXiv.abstract: Conversational assistants are expected to help people with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and communication styles. Yet evaluations centered on a single cooperative user provide limited insight into how reliably an assistant serves users with different personas. We introduce PersonaChatBench, a framework for evaluating task competence and responsiveness to diverse user needs. PersonaChatBench pairs the same underlying task with multiple simulated users, each guided by a private persona card that specifies distinct needs, preferences, and interaction behaviors. By holding the task fixed while varying the user, the framework examines how assistant performance changes across user conditions. We evaluate 20 language models across six domains, separately assessing native task outcomes, fulfillment of expressed persona needs, and simulator fidelity. Our results show that task performance and need fulfillment vary across personas and domains. Strong task performance does not necessarily translate into satisfying individual needs, and models' relative strengths in meeting those needs are not consistent across domains. PersonaChatBench makes these differences measurable, revealing gaps obscured by aggregate scores and helping identify which users an assistant serves well and where adaptation is needed. It provides a basis for evaluating consistency across users and guiding the development of assistants that better accommodate diverse needs in everyday applications.

arXiv.title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results
arXiv.comments: 47 pages, 1 figure, 14 tables. Includes Appendix A
arXiv.abstract: AI answers require more than apparent correctness: reviewers need to inspect their recorded basis. We introduce the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation. We reference KLM v0.3 (repository tag v0.3.0). Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author-reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work.

arXiv.title: Two choices suffice: $k$-out sampling leaves $O(n/k)$ intercomponent edges for $k\geq 2$
arXiv.abstract: Given a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices, random $k$-out sampling forms a spanning subgraph by having each vertex independently choose $k$ incident edges uniformly with replacement. We prove that, for every integer $k\geq2$, the expected number of original edges joining distinct sampled components is $O(n/k)$. This resolves the conjecture of Holm, King, Thorup, Zamir, and Zwick in its full range, improving their logarithmic sampling requirement to the optimal threshold of two choices per vertex. The bound fails for $k=1$, and the dependence $O(n/k)$ is tight up to constant factors. Our result holds with replacement and consequently also without replacement. In particular, this implies that contracting just two independent local choices per vertex suffices to reduce an arbitrary simple graph to a quotient with $O(n)$ edges in expectation, which is crucial in reducing the instance size for many contraction-based algorithms. Our proof uses switching arguments to relate intercomponent edges to bridges and a degree-weighted component potential, whose expectation we also bound with a switching argument.

arXiv.title: RAMA: Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Routing with Episodic Memory for LEO Satellite Networks
arXiv.abstract: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.

arXiv.title: The Quartic Gap Between Quantum and Dequantized Algorithms for Linear Algebra Is Tight
arXiv.abstract: Quantum algorithms for linear algebra that access a matrix $A$ through quantum random access memory (QRAM) prepare quantum states proportional to the solutions of linear systems and related problems. Dequantized classical algorithms, when given sampling and query access to $A$, return sampling and query access to an approximate solution. Both kinds of algorithms use a number of queries that is polynomial in the normalized Frobenius norm $ρ=\|A\|_F/\|A\|$ and does not directly depend on the dimension. For linear systems at fixed condition number and accuracy, quantum algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ)$ queries, whereas the best dequantized algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ^4)$. We prove that this quartic gap is tight in the worst case, up to a logarithmic factor. For every constant $κ_0>1$, we construct dense linear systems with condition number at most $κ_0$ for which sampling from the solution within a sufficiently small constant total variation distance requires $Ω(ρ^4/\logρ)$ classical queries but only $Θ(ρ)$ quantum queries. The same separation holds, for errors below smaller thresholds, for positive-definite systems, least squares, ridge regression, matrix powers and square roots, imaginary-time and real-time Hamiltonian evolution, and sampling from the top principal component. Our results therefore show that many quantum algorithms for linear algebra, achieve a near-quartic speedup in the worst case, over classical algorithms with sampling and query access. All of these classical lower bounds follow from the same framework, which is based on a lower bound for sampling from distributions that depend on a fixed set of Fourier coefficients of an unknown Boolean function.

arXiv.title: Stochastic Rayleigh-Ritz Ascent: Global Linear Convergence under a Spectral Gap
arXiv.abstract: We consider the adjoint-free random-plane iteration algorithm for finding the top eigenvector of a matrix proposed in (SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 47 (2026), 1349-1374). Unlike standard methods such as the power method or gradient descent, the above algorithm lacked linear convergence guarantees in the presence of a spectral gap. In this paper, we establish explicit spectral-gap-dependent global linear convergence rates in expectation, providing quantitative guarantees for the empirically observed convergence.

arXiv.title: Measurement-Based Assessment of Decadal Inertia and Primary Frequency Response Trends in the US Eastern Interconnection
arXiv.comments: Presented in CIGRE 2026 Grid of the Future Symposium.The paper has 12 pages and 6 figures in total
arXiv.abstract: Changes in the generation mix of the U.S. Eastern Interconnection (EI) raise questions about long-term frequency performance, particularly inertia and primary frequency response (PFR). This paper jointly examines these characteristics using synchronized FNET/GridEye frequency measurements and confirmed generation-trip events from 2013 to 2025. A representative EI frequency trajectory is constructed using the median of geographically distributed measurements. Effective inertia is estimated quarterly from the early post-disturbance rate of change of frequency (RoCoF), using a 3-second window and least-squares fitting. PFR is evaluated using the beta metric, which measures aggregate frequency response from disturbance size and the A-to-B frequency deviation. Annual beta estimates are obtained after filtering events by starting frequency and disturbance size to improve comparability across years. Results show that EI effective inertia varies seasonally and follows a non-monotonic trend rather than a uniform long-term decline. Over the same period, coal generation decreased while natural gas, wind, and solar generation increased. Changes in synchronous generator commitment and operating conditions may have offset some expected inertia reductions. Filtered beta generally increased from the mid-2010s to the early 2020s, with year-to-year variability thereafter. The different trends show that early inertial behavior and broader aggregate frequency response have not evolved in parallel. Joint analysis of inertia and beta offers a more complete measurement-based assessment of EI frequency performance during the generation transition.

arXiv.title: Implicit Additively Weighted Geodesic Voronoi Diagrams and Applications
arXiv.abstract: Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $m$ vertices. After $O(m)$-time preprocessing of $P$, for any set $S$ of $n$ additively weighted point sites, we compute an implicit additively weighted geodesic Voronoi diagram in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time, supporting nearest-neighbor queries in $O(\log(n+m))$ time. In contrast, explicitly constructing the diagram requires $Ω(m)$ time. Our algorithm introduces a new sweep-line paradigm that avoids explicitly constructing the diagram, together with a novel technique for point location in implicit subdivisions. As applications, we obtain new dynamic data structures for additively weighted geodesic nearest-neighbor searching and the first efficient algorithms for shortest paths in geodesic disk graphs. After the same $O(m)$-time preprocessing, single-source shortest paths in a geodesic disk graph of $n$ sites can be computed in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time in the unweighted case and $O(n^{3/2}(\log n+\log^2 m))$ time in the weighted case. We also extend our techniques to implicit farthest geodesic Voronoi diagrams for unweighted sites, obtaining analogous bounds and dynamic farthest-neighbor data structures.

arXiv.title: Embodied Movable Antennas
arXiv.abstract: This paper introduces embodied movable antennas (MAs), a new MA architecture that rethinks the source of antenna mobility. Unlike conventional MAs that rely on dedicated antenna actuators, embodied MAs harness the mechanical degrees of freedom already present in physical agents to reconfigure antenna position and orientation. We distinguish two modes of embodied MAs: task-coupled and task-preserving. Focusing on the latter, we show how wireless channels can be reconfigured by exploiting task-equivalent host configurations without altering the prescribed physical task. Using a redundant robotic manipulator as a canonical realization, we characterize the intrinsically coupled antenna translation and orientation induced by task-preserving self-motion and derive an exact Fourier representation of the resulting multipath channel. Our analysis reveals that the wireless value of embodied mobility depends not merely on how far an antenna can move, but on which configurations remain feasible under the physical task and how their coupled motion interacts with polarization and multipath propagation. Building on this insight, we develop a cross-task antenna mounting design that enables wireless adaptation with a fixed physical installation. Numerical results demonstrate substantial communication gains through task-preserving motion. These findings establish mechanical redundancy as a new, quantifiable resource for wireless channel reconfiguration.

arXiv.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data from Sliced Chebyshev Moments
arXiv.abstract: Research on practical differentially private (DP) synthetic data has largely focused on methods that approximately preserve low-dimensional marginals of a target distribution, and can thus only hope to preserve higher-dimensional, global structure as a lucky by-product. At the same time, existing methods that target global accuracy guarantees pay a price exponential in the data dimension, $d$. In this work, we address this ``curse of dimensionality'' by presenting a new DP synthetic data algorithm, SPLICE, that comes with a compelling global distributional guarantee, even in high-dimensions, and moreover, is practically state-of-the-art. Our algorithm is based on measuring noisy sliced Chebyshev polynomial moments of the target distribution and fitting a distribution to match, a twist on recent polynomial methods for 1-D synthetic data. We prove that, given a dataset of $n$ examples, SPLICE returns a private distribution with Sliced Wasserstein-1 distance $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ from the target, for constant privacy parameters. Notably, this bound is independent of the data dimension, $d$. Along the way, we prove a moment matching result of independent interest: for a distribution on the unit ball, matching the first $O(1/α)$ Chebyshev moments along $\tilde{O}(d/α^2)$ random directions guarantees $α$ Sliced Wasserstein error. Finally, we provide a practical implementation of the algorithm that borrows tools from the tensor decomposition literature and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior DP synthetic data methods on an extensive benchmark.

arXiv.title: Think in 360°: Benchmarking and Bootstrapping Panoramic Video Reasoning
arXiv.abstract: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.

arXiv.title: RangeSWA: Training-Free Length Extrapolation for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
arXiv.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.

arXiv.title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?
arXiv.abstract: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. This rule, EI stopping, never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing in the surrogate raises EI stopping's utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.

arXiv.title: Dirichlet form approach to stochastic thin-film equations
arXiv.abstract: The thin-film equation describes the evolution of a thin liquid film driven by capillarity and limited by viscosity. For sufficiently small film heights, thermal fluctuations may not be neglected. Since the thin-film equation as an overdamped evolution equation has a gradient flow structure, the informal implementation of the fluctuation-dissipation principle is straightforward. In this paper, we work out that the concept of Dirichlet forms and the related construction of Markov processes are tailor-made for this type of overdamped continuum evolution with thermal noise. However, the concept of Dirichlet forms relies on the availability of a Gibbsian equilibrium measure, which, in case of the thin-film equation, limits the treatment to the $(1+1)$-dimensional case. By means of Dirichlet form theory, we obtain the existence and uniqueness of the evolution of laws on configuration space. We show that the regularity of the realizations of this Markov process matches the heuristics. In a simplified situation with a Gaussian reference measure and a non-degenerate mobility function, we characterize it as what is called an energy solution. The latter provides a pathwise decomposition of the driving forces into a deterministic and a thermal one, which was the starting point. Applying the same techniques in the spatially discretized setting proposed in [Math. Comp. 92 (2023), 1931--1976], we obtain the same results uniformly in the discretization parameter. In particular, Galerkin as well as spectral approximations of the stochastic thin-film equation are shown to be uniformly tight in optimal topologies. In the simplified setting, we also prove Mosco convergence of the associated Dirichlet forms and thereby obtain convergence of these approximations.

arXiv.title: From Scalar Games to Unconstrained Network Zero-Sum Games: Transfer Principles for Gradient-Based Learning
arXiv.abstract: We show that, for a broad class of gradient-based learning rules, scalar zero-sum games form a complete test family for convergence in unconstrained network zero-sum games. Specifically, suppose a learning rule achieves last-iterate or time-average convergence on every scalar game of magnitude $a$ whenever $η\leq f(a)$, where $f$ is nonincreasing. Then the same guarantee holds on an arbitrary network zero-sum game with stacked game operator $\mathbf{G}$ whenever $η\leq f(\lVert\mathbf{G}\rVert_2)$. More generally, finite-time rate guarantees transfer mode by mode: the network response is bounded by the largest response of its scalar canonical games, and under compatible linear initialization conventions the worst-case finite-time network response is exactly the largest scalar canonical rate. Thus, understanding the learning dynamics on scalar games is sufficient to characterize universal convergence and worst-case rates over the corresponding class of network games. The result follows from the classical planar decomposition of real skew-symmetric game operators. Related mode-wise reasoning has appeared implicitly in spectral analyses of particular learning algorithms and in prior work using these decompositions for game representation and visualization; here we isolate the resulting transfer principle for gradient-based learning. We discuss implications for simplifying convergence analysis, time-average guarantees, low-dimensional geometric arguments, accelerated-method design, and worst-case numerical testing.

arXiv.title: Rethinking Asymmetry in Self-Supervised 3D Geometry Learning
arXiv.abstract: Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training.

arXiv.title: A General Theoretical Framework for Transformed Geometric Pattern Matching in Music
arXiv.comments: 61 pages; 23 figures; draft of second chapter of forthcoming book
arXiv.abstract: In this paper, we present a framework of concepts, terminology and notation for geometric pattern matching, centred around the idea of a {\em transformation class}. After formally defining the concept of a transformation class, we provide detailed definitions of a number of specific transformation classes that are particularly relevant to pattern matching and pattern discovery in music, which is the primary application domain within which the framework has been developed. We then provide formal definitions of the notions of {\em match}, {\em occurrence}, {\em maximal match\/} and {\em maximal occurrence\/} and prove some results relating to these concepts. We then define and explore in detail the idea of an {\em occurrence set\/} and the more general notion of a {\em heterogeneous occurrence set}. Finally, we explore in detail the concept of {\em transformational equivalence}, including a consideration of {\em transformation groups}, along with the group-theoretic and transformational equivalence properties of selected transformation classes.

arXiv.title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
arXiv.abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.

arXiv.title: Towards Understanding the Impact of Plasticity Loss on Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Environments
arXiv.comments: 9 pages main paper, 15 pages references and appendix, 17 figures. Presented at the Nineteenth European Workshop on Reinforcement Learning (EWRL 2026)
arXiv.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful framework for sequential decision-making. Despite many high-profile successes in recent years, deep RL is known to be brittle. An emerging line of research attributes this brittleness to a loss of plasticity in neural networks. However, plasticity loss has so far been understudied in stochastic environments. We study this interplay systematically, training SAC agents on three DeepMind Control tasks augmented with controlled levels of observation and action noise. We find that plasticity-preserving methods increase learning robustness on the two harder tasks, with their advantage growing as observation noise increases, while combining resets with layer normalization underperforms resets alone at every observation noise level tested. Further, stochasticity can accelerate the loss of plasticity in harder environments, whereas in easier settings noise can act as a regularizer that sustains plasticity. Lastly, plasticity loss is most pronounced in the early stages of training. In the most challenging stochastic settings, TD instability rather than gradual plasticity loss becomes the dominant failure mode.

arXiv.title: The Pareto Secretary Problem
arXiv.comments: 48 pages, 8 figures. A preliminary version has been accepted to WINE 2026
arXiv.abstract: The Pareto secretary problem asks for online selection of a Pareto-maximal observation from an i.i.d. sample: no other observation is at least as good in every coordinate and strictly better in one. For every fixed dimension $d\ge2$ and independent continuous coordinates, the optimal failure probability is of order $1/[(\log n)^{d-1}\log\log n]$, both with full information and with coordinate ranks alone. A deterministic rank rule attains the optimal leading term uniformly over the marginals. For every fixed positive definite Gaussian covariance, the same failure order holds, with a leading constant depending on the correlation matrix, and a rank-based rule attains the optimal leading failure probability without knowing the Gaussian parameters. In both models, we determine the optimal fixed cutoff and its leading failure constant; its failure probability exceeds the unrestricted optimum by a factor $Θ_d((\log\log n)^2)$. Under arbitrary dependence, a fixed joint density with uniform marginals can instead have optimal full-information success tending to approximately $0.58$. The proof uses the scarcity of observations with very small domination probability to bound every stopping rule. A matching rule selects a currently maximal point when this probability is below a threshold that increases as time runs out. Coordinate ranks from an initial sample provide sufficiently accurate estimates to preserve the optimal leading failure probability. For singular Gaussian distributions with known correlations, we characterize the optimal failure asymptotics attainable using ranks. Singular dependence can make every observation acceptable or recover the difficulty of selecting a single best point.

arXiv.title: Hyperbolic Inverse Reinforcement Learning
arXiv.abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to infer the reward function underlying observed behavior, but its predictive accuracy and interpretability depend on how that reward is computed from the underlying features. While prior IRL reward functions have been implemented through a variety of techniques including linear weights, neural networks, or other function approximators, none make assumptions about the geometry of the underlying feature space. Inspired by geometric organization observed in neural circuits, we introduce Hyperbolic inverse reinforcement learning (Hyperbolic IRL), which parameterizes reward as a function of Hyperbolic distance between the feature vector and a learned parameter vector, as well as its Euclidean distance variant. We tested our methods against a range of linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under both deterministic and stochastic policies. Our Hyperbolic approach achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on established benchmarks and excelled in the low data limit and across dense environments. Applied to human navigation among multiple exhibits in a museum room, Hyperbolic IRL reveals reward structure that depends not only on individual exhibit-distance features, but also on non-separable conjunctions between them. Together, these results demonstrate that a Hyperbolic reward parameterization can improve both the predictive accuracy and interpretability of IRL, providing a framework for studying how non-separable, conjunctive structure can begin to explain behavior.

arXiv.title: Strategic Tanking in Stable Matching Markets
arXiv.abstract: Motivated by a broad literature in psychology, organizational behavior, and matching markets, we introduce strategic tanking: an agent deliberately makes themselves less attractive to selected potential partners in order to improve their eventual assignment. Unlike traditional manipulation in stable matching, a tanker does not misreport whom they prefer; instead, they influence how others rank them. We show that tanking has a striking connection to classical preference manipulation. Cutoff tanking, in which an agent tanks with every potential partner below a chosen threshold, has exactly the same effect on the stable set as truncating one's own preference list at that threshold. Thus an agent can reproduce the power of a classical truncation while leaving their own preferences unchanged and every match acceptable. Arbitrary tanking, however, can go substantially further: under proposer-deferred acceptance, tanking equilibria can lie outside the sincere stable set. More broadly, whenever the sincere stable set contains multiple matchings, profitable strategic behavior remains available through either traditional preference manipulation or tanking, even when one side is restricted to honestly reporting their own preferences.

arXiv.title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)
arXiv.comments: 6 pages, 3 figures, In proceedings of 1st international Symposium on AI and Fluid Mechanics 2025 (Paper No. S11P2)
arXiv.abstract: Physics informed machine learning provides a framework to study and simulate fluid dynamics, potentially at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional numerical methods, with the goal of improving the explainability, accuracy and robustness of purely data driven machine learning methods. In this work, we extend the hard constraint projection (HCP) method developed by Chen et al. [Journal of Computational Physics, 445, 110624, 2021] from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to a nonlinear PDE: the 1D Burgers' equation. To strictly impose a discrete approximation of the governing equation, the Burgers' equation is first locally discretised (using a finite difference stencil) then decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix. Using tools from linear algebra, the constraint matrix is used to construct a projection matrix. A physics informed neural network (PINN) [Raissi et al. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686, 2019] is used to predict the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects the velocity prediction to the hyperplane of exact solutions to a discretised form of the Burgers' equation. Our initial results indicate that the HCP-PINN initially trains similarly to an equivalent PINN, and as the PINN loss plateaus, the HCP-PINN loss continues to decline. When tested on a previously unseen uniform grid of points covering the domain, the HCP-PINN exhibits higher accuracy, converging to a data error approximately an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN. We also observe that the inclusion of the HCP layer results in better observance of the governing PDE. Our findings suggest that the HCP-PINN can be more robust to the selection of physics collocation points, and less dependent on collocation point quantity.

arXiv.title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression
arXiv.abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $κ$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(κ\varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.

arXiv.title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
arXiv.abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.

arXiv.title: Fast Privacy Loss Accounting for Random Allocation via Multiscale FFT
arXiv.abstract: In the random allocation sampling scheme each user's data is used in $k$ steps chosen randomly and uniformly from a sequence of $t$ steps. This scheme is known to improve on Poisson sampling in private optimization and in communication-efficient aggregation. The existing privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant for this scheme runs in time quadratic in the inverse of the accuracy parameter $α$ (Feldman and Shenfeld, 2026). We give an algorithm, \emph{multiscale FFT}, that represents likelihood ratios on a grid that is uniform within each dyadic interval and computes the exact rounding of every pairwise sum using FFTs within each interval. It keeps the guarantees of the accountant and improves the dependence of its running time on $α$ from $O(α^{-2})$ to $O(α^{-1}\log(1/α))$. In addition, we demonstrate that rounding can be performed via the mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection of (Doroshenko et al., 2026). This reduces the errors that rounding introduces in the mean of the privacy loss and in the $χ^2$ divergence of the computed pair from the order of $α$ to $O(α^2/\log(t))$. In our experiments, our algorithm achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude at high accuracy and gives improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.

arXiv.title: Gradient Descent on Two ReLU Neurons: Global Landscape and Bifurcation Dynamics
arXiv.abstract: Understanding how gradient descent learns features remains a central challenge in neural network theory. We study this question in a minimal multi-index setting that already exhibits rich multi-phase gradient dynamics: a well-specified two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model under isotropic Gaussian inputs, trained by population gradient flow from small initialization. We show that the dynamics are organized by two directions: the "easy" bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and the "hard" splitting direction, which governs specialization. To characterize the loss structure and learning behavior, we analyze the population squared-loss landscape and show that every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle. We then track the gradient-flow trajectory, showing that student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle before escaping and specializing to teacher neurons. Our results provide both a landscape and dynamics account of the multi-phase symmetry-breaking behavior that arises in a simple multi-index model and under standard algorithmic and architectural choices.

arXiv.title: Functional Tensor Trains for High-Order Greeks and Exposure Tails of Multi-Asset Structured Products
arXiv.abstract: Risk management of worst-of autocallables needs price sensitivities (Greeks) up to third order and the potential future exposure, a tail quantile of the note's future value. In Monte Carlo, each order of differentiation multiplies the sampling noise by a factor that grows with the observation frequency, and nested simulation turns the noise of its inner paths into a bias of the quantile. We instead solve the backward pricing recursion, storing the continuation value as an $hp$ functional tensor train (hp-FTT) whose piecewise-polynomial cores are split at the barriers, so that worst-of barrier events act exactly, with rank one. For Gaussian transitions we show that the polynomial degree sufficient for an error $\varepsilon$ grows only as $\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}$. One solve then gives every Greek at any spot without sampling noise, by integrating the likelihood-ratio weight against the stored value, and the values it stores at future dates replace inner simulation. Against the strongest Monte Carlo estimators we could build or find published, on worst-of autocallables observed monthly on three to five assets, the order of the Greek and the accuracy decide which method is cheaper. At $1\%$ accuracy Monte Carlo is more than an order of magnitude cheaper for deltas, second-order Greeks go either way, and hp-FTT is cheaper for every third-order Greek, by up to two orders of magnitude. At $0.1\%$ hp-FTT is cheaper for every Greek we could check, under geometric Brownian motion and local volatility alike. For the exposure alone Monte Carlo is cheaper at $1\%$ and hp-FTT at $0.1\%$, and a solve run for the Greeks yields it for little more than scenario sampling. Sampling pays in variance for each derivative and hp-FTT in rank for each asset, so Monte Carlo keeps low-order Greeks at percent accuracy, rarely observed contracts and many assets.

arXiv.title: Where ADS Crashes Differ: A Harmonized Comparison Against Human Baselines
arXiv.abstract: Crash-rate comparisons between automated driving systems (ADS) and human drivers require an exposure denominator that only a few operators publish. We instead ask a composition question: given a crash, does the mix of crash types differ between ADS and human-driven vehicles? The question needs no mileage and can therefore cover every ADS operator. We assemble the NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO) ADS incident files across both file generations into 2,450 distinct in-scope incidents (2021-2026), of which 828 fall within the 2021-2024 window covered by the Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS), the national police-reported human comparator. A schema-constrained large language model (LLM) codes each SGO narrative into the CRSS crash-type taxonomy. Because SGO compels reporting far below the police-reporting threshold, we bracket reportability with an objective severity floor and a reasonable-person rubric, and claim a difference only where it survives both. Two composition differences hold under every reportability definition, tow definition and weighting of the human side, and under both definitions of driverless operation: turn-across-path crashes are under-represented among ADS crashes (0.23-0.46x the CRSS share under the primary driverless definition) and so are single-vehicle crashes (0.19-0.56x). In severity-floor rear-end crashes the ADS vehicle is the striking party at a quasi-induced-exposure ratio of 0.121 (95% CI [0.05, 0.23]) against a human baseline of 1.000. If the ADS vehicle is also struck more often than its exposure implies, this ratio overstates the ADS-human difference. We also document three pitfalls in the federal data: an operator-specific coding of driverless operation, a tow-away criterion confounded by fleet recovery practice, and an occupancy confound that accounts for about 42% of the apparent ADS-human severity gap.

arXiv.title: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions
arXiv.comments: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary material available as an ancillary file
arXiv.abstract: Objective: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity. Materials and Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant. Results: Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3-R2 -0.00257, 95% CI -0.00370 to -0.00146), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision (-0.00012, 95% CI -0.00206 to +0.00208). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful. Discussion: Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements. Conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs.

arXiv.title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
arXiv.abstract: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19--23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running $24.5\times$ faster on TREC DL and $16.7\times$ faster on BRIGHT.

arXiv.title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger
arXiv.categories: cs.LG cs.IT math.IT math.ST stat.ML stat.TH
arXiv.abstract: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's.

arXiv.title: A Better Critic Matters for Distribution Matching Distillation
arXiv.comments: 35 pages, 16 figures. Project page and code: https://peppaking8.github.io/critic-matters/
arXiv.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student using the difference between a teacher's score and an online critic's estimate of the student distribution's score. We investigate what the critic needs, in capacity and in information, to provide a reliable training signal. On the capacity side, controlled experiments across seven SiT model sizes on ImageNet show that increasing teacher size while keeping a small critic fixed can degrade student quality and cause training collapse. Scaling the critic alongside the teacher, a strategy we call joint scaling, prevents collapse in our experiments and allows the student to benefit from larger teachers. On the information side, rather than forcing the critic to model a step-agnostic mixture of student outputs, we introduce a step-aware critic (STAC) that conditions on the student's generation step to estimate step-specific scores. Together, joint scaling and STAC consistently improve few-step distillation across class-conditional ImageNet generation, text-to-image generation with SDXL and FLUX.2, and text-to-video generation with Wan2.1.

arXiv.title: ReLift: Dense 3D Tracking as Lifted Trajectory Repair
arXiv.abstract: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.

arXiv.title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches
arXiv.abstract: In many practical deployments of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the server processes data in batches. Randomly sampling these batches allows for better privacy bounds via privacy amplification results. Most sampling schemes with provable privacy amplification, including Poisson sampling and random allocation, result in variable batch sizes. The privacy guarantee of these schemes requires that the batch sizes are not revealed. In distributed settings, the server performing the aggregation or any party observing the communication traffic may learn these batch sizes. Furthermore, in both centralized and distributed settings, memory and computation constraints may require each batch to be of some maximum size $s$, necessitating truncation of the batch when it exceeds this limit. It is known that this truncation can result in a significant increase in privacy loss. In this work, we address both of these challenges via a simple mechanism that uses a random number of \emph{dummy points} to privatize the batch size and maintain the privacy guarantee even under truncation. We demonstrate that our mechanism is easy to implement in a distributed setting, and provide a general analysis of this mechanism for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Our analysis is designed to support efficient and relatively tight privacy accounting. It also effectively amplifies the privacy of the count releases by subsampling, making the expected number of dummy points asymptotically smaller than what is needed to directly privatize the (sensitivity-one) batch sizes with non-negative noise. For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, we demonstrate empirically that our mechanism achieves better privacy--efficiency tradeoffs than the direct accounting for truncation recently given by (Ganesh, 2025).

arXiv.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
arXiv.abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy.
